Finally, TestCTRL generates syntactically correct, semantically meaningful, and comprehensive tests with high code coverage. We leverage the Defects4J benchmark to evaluate our approach. Compared with existing test generation approaches and fine-tuned LLMs (e.g., AthenaTest [63] and StarCoder [33]), our ex- perimental results show that TestCTRL can substantially improve the compilation pass rate, line coverage, and branch coverage of tests generated by LLMs. Compared with the best-performed baseline (i.e., StarCoder [33] with more than 15.5B parameters), TestCTRL increases the line and branch coverage by 88.42% and 88.25%, respectively. We further evaluate the impact of TestCTRL on the bug detection performance of the test generation model. The experimental results show that TestCTRL improves the performance of bug detection, increasing the number of detected bugs by 128.57%. In summary, the main contributions of this article are as follows: —We create a new dataset enriched with the CoT prompt. This dataset comprises over 96K focal methods, corresponding tests, and the associated CoT prompts. To the best of our knowledge, it is the first test generation dataset with CoT prompts. —We propose TestCTRL, a novel LLM-based unit test generation approach that leverages the CoT prompt and deep RL strategy to generate unit tests. —We conduct comprehensive experiments using the Defects4J benchmark. Evaluation results show that TestCTRL outperforms all baselines. —We release TestCTRL with a comprehensive replication package [47] that encompasses the source code, the curated CoT prompt, and detailed evaluation results. Finally, we conclude our study and shed light on potential future directions in Section7. 2 Background This section introduces the background knowledge of fine-tuning LLMs with CoT prompts and deep RL. 2.1 Fine-Tuning LLMs with Prompts Our approach employs the CoT prompt to enhance LLMs’ capacity to handle intricate reasoning tasks. The CoT prompt refers to a series of intermediate natural language reasoning steps that lead tothefinal output. Thefinaloutput ofTestCTRLisa setof unittests. Itsimulates thehuman thought process when solving complicated reasoning tasks. The prompt typically decomposes the problem into intermediate steps and solves each step before giving the final answer. CoT prompt tuning can be seen as a special form of prompt learning whose core principle is to align the training objectives of specific downstream tasks with the foundational pre-training phase of LLMs, as introduced in previous work [36]. Different from the standard way of prompting language models where a set of (query, answer) pairs are given as demonstrations [5], CoT prompt tuning also includes a rationale for each example, encouraging the model to verbalize the intermediate reasoning steps for solving the task. Figure1 shows the framework of TestCTRL, consisting of two main stages: the fine-tuning and inference phases. The fine-tuning phase is designed to train TestCTRL by leveraging two modules, a policy model and a reward model, with the following four steps. (1)CoT Dataset Creation: We use GPT-3.5 to construct a CoT dataset. Given a focal method, GPT-3.5 generates the intention and possible test inputs of the focal method. We introduce the step of creating the CoT dataset in Section3.1. (2)Policy Model Fine-Tuning: These outputs are concatenated with the focal method and used to fine-tune CodeLlama-7B [56], which serves as the policy model. Section3.2 presents the policy model. (3)Reward Model Fine-Tuning: Another LLM, CodeGPT [9, 37], is fine-tuned to serve as the reward model. The reward model evaluates the generated unit tests (from the policy model) by predicting their line coverage rate for the focal method. The predicted line coverage rate is used as a reward signal. Section3.3 introduces the reward model. (4)Policy Model Optimization: The policy model (CodeLlama-7B) is further opti- mized using PPO, with the reward model providing the coverage-based reward signals. Section3.4 illustrates the PPO algorithm to optimize the policy model in RL. This iterative process refines the policy model, ultimately producing the trained TestCTRL. In such cases, a predictive model offers a lightweight, approximated alternative for early stage test generation. While calculating actual coverage is not computationally prohibitive for standard setups, environments with limited computational resources might prefer a predictive model to reduce cost and complexity. To simulate test execution without running the program and return the coverage calculated after the simulated execution of the test, we propose to fine-tune an LLM to predict coverage without running the test code. LLMs have gained prominence in code-related tasks and demonstrated impressive results. Besides, code coverage in software testing measures the total amount of program code executed by a set of tests. It is a quantifiable metric that provides clear and objective feedback to LLMs through an RL strategy. Higher code coverage implies that a more significant portion of the code statements in focal methods are executed when tests are run. As LLM generates new tests and receives feedback, it can incrementally improve the tests to cover more code statements. There are multiple coverage metrics, including line and branch coverage. Compared to the branch coverage, the line coverage is relatively uncomplicated, which merely verifies if every line or code statement has been executed. A good reward metric needs to be easily calculated. Hence, we choose the line coverage as the reward score and initialize the reward model using fine-tuned LLM based on the line coverage. Line coverage is simpler to calculate and interpret than stronger metrics like branch or path coverage. It provides a straightforward initial signal for policy optimization. The use of line coverage could be positioned as a stepping stone for exploring more sophisticated metrics in future work. Intuitively, the greater the coverage, the feedback given by the reward model increases. This means that the rewards returned by the model should increase with coverage. In addition, we compare the execution-based and prediction-based code coverage methods in terms of time efficiency, memory consumption, and accuracy. Specifically, the prediction-based method requires only 0.0366 seconds to compute coverage, which is faster than the execution- based approach that takes 16.89 seconds. This substantial reduction in computation time highlights the efficiency of the prediction-based method, particularly in scenarios where rapid feedback is essential. With respect to memory usage, the prediction-based method consumes 987.46 MB, compared to 0.56 MB for the execution-based method. Although the prediction-based approach requires more memory, the tradeoff is considered acceptable given its notable advantage in speed. In terms of accuracy, the prediction-based method yields a slightly higher MSE of 1.05% compared to the execution-based method, as shown in Section4.4.3. However, this minor loss in accuracy is often tolerable in large-scale or time-sensitive applications, where the need for real-time performance and fast test generation outweighs the marginal decrease in precision. We follow previous research [63] and employ a dataset that includes focal methods, their tests, and associated line coverage to train the reward model. The line coverage is in percentage form, a scalar value that indicates the amount of code (lines, branches, etc.) exercised by the test case relative to the total executable code. For example, if a method contains 10 executable lines and 7 are covered, the coverage percentage is 0.7. A single scalar value is easy to calculate, store, and use as a prediction target. It is consistent with the reward mechanism in RL, where the scalar value is directly used for optimization. Code coverage is calculated using the Cobertura tool [8]. Focal methods in the dataset are derived from multiple Java software projects of various coding styles and complexity. (1)CoT Dataset: We define the dataset comprising focal methods paired with CoT prompts as the CoT dataset, which is derived from the Methods2Test benchmark [63]. The original dataset consisted of 780,944 test cases. To improve its quality, we refer to previous work [1, 74], remove duplicate tests, and filter out those with bad patterns. Bad patterns in the context of the dataset refer to characteristics or structures in the test code that make them unrepresentative of typical, high-quality unit tests, uninformative for training a model to generate useful tests, or potentially misleading for the downstream tasks (e.g., CoT prompt generation or fine-tuning). Specifically, we exclude the “Indented Test,” a test whose code includes decision points, loops, “conditional statements,” or “print statements.” “Indented Test” refers to tests containing deeply nested structures, such as loops or multiple levels of conditionals. Unit tests are typically concise and focused on small, specific scenarios. Tests with deep nesting may be more indicative of integration or system tests rather than unit tests. Deeply indented structures might introduce unnecessary noise into the dataset, making it harder for the model to generalize patterns of good test writing. Besides, tests with loops might inadvertently introduce infinite execution scenarios or complicate coverage calculation during training. To maintain a cleaner and more representative dataset for model training, we excluded test cases containing two or more levels of nested loops, re- tainingonlythosewithasinglelevelofnesting.Thisdecisionwasmadetoensurethatthegenerated tests remain simple and aligned with the core principles of unit testing. We excluded tests with bad patterns, including tests containing only print statements, tests lacking assertions, and tests with overly complex structures (e.g., deeply nested loops). These patterns are removed as they are unrep- resentative of high-quality unit tests and could negatively impact the model’s ability to generalize. This dataset is used as a training dataset for fine-tuning the policy model. Specifically, we recruited two Ph.D. students, none of whom are co-authors of the study. Each student specializing in either software engineering or computer science has at least 3 years of Java programming experience. We created a questionnaire based on 100 focal methods randomly selected from the CoT prompt for a detailed evaluation. Each question provides comprehensive details of the focal method, including its body, associated unit tests, project repository link, and precise file location. Inspired by previous research [28], participants were guided to evaluate the quality of the prompt across two key dimensions:relevance and diversity. We adopted a scoring schema for each dimension, from −1 to 1, where−1 represents the CoT prompt appearing irrelevant and monotonous compared to focal methods, 0 represents that the correlation and diversity between CoT prompts and focal methodsareunclear,and1representsthattheCoTpromptandfocalmethodsshowclearcorrelation and diversity. The questionnaire incorporated sample items to facilitate participant assessment where the focal methods and their associated CoT prompts demonstrated relevance and diversity. Participants subsequently rated each CoT prompt using the provided example as the baseline. The quality assessment data from human evaluation is included in our replication package [47] to enhance transparency and enable a more comprehensive analysis of the models’ performance. One such threat is dataset bias. One of the major concerns is the potential bias of CoT and reward datasets from public Java projects. Although these large datasets may capture a wide variety of Java unit testing patterns, there is still a risk of overfitting to specific application types. To address this threat, we plan to incorporate other programming languages in future evaluations of our approach. Besides, one threat isdata leakage. CodeLlama and other LLMs have been trained on a large number of code corpus collected from GitHub [20], and this dataset is unreleased. Since the projects in Defects4J ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology, Vol. 35, No. 4, Article 92. Publication date: March 2026. In this case, overfitting may cause evaluation results to be biased. Given the low quality of generated test cases by CodeLlama-7B without fine-tuning, the data leakage threat is likely to be insignificant. Meanwhile, TestCTRL performs better than CodeLlama-7B without fine-tuning (see the experimental results in Section4.3), indicating the advantages of TestCTRL. In addition, we mitigated the threat by filtering the CoT dataset. Another threat ishuman bias. Differences in testing experiences among participants could introduce inconsistencies in our results. To address this, we ask participants with different testing backgrounds to evaluate the same focal method. The high observed inter-rater agreement indicates the resilience of TestCTRL against this potential bias. Threats to External Validity refers to the extent to which research findings can be generalized to other settings. There are three threats: (1)Model Generalizability: The ChatGPT version we use is GPT-3.5-turbo-0613, and the cutoff time for its training dataset is September 2021. We mainly utilize CodeLlama-7B [10] as the policy model and adopt CodeGPT [9] as the reward model. The update time of CodeLlama-7B is March 2024. The update time of CodeGPT-7B is September 2020. Although these models are benchmarked and widely recognized for their performance, this choice could raise concerns about the generalizability of our findings. Nevertheless, the consistent performance of both CodeLlama and CodeGPT in various situations reduces this threat. (2)Hyper- Parameter Optimization: Due to hardware limitations, exhaustive hyper-parameter optimization is not feasible. To maintain consistency, we adopt hyper-parameter values recorded in previous studies [33]. (3)Reproducibility: Our reliance on OpenAI models for CoT prompt generation may raise reproducibility concerns. To increase transparency, we outlined the instructions for the CoT prompt generation and provided access to the fixed-principle dataset we crafted. Future work will seek to diversify the LLMs used, ensuring our approach remains robust. 6 Related Work Learning-Based Unit Test Generation. Learning-based test generation approaches leverage DL tech- niques to generate unit tests [14, 32, 40, 41, 63, 66]. They treat the test generation task as a neural machine translation problem, training a model to translate the focal method into the corresponding test prefix or test assertion. Early research [14, 40, 66] focuses on generating assertions. They either train DL models or fine-tune LLMs using assertion generation datasets. The given test prefix is used with the focal method as input, and the corresponding assertion is the output. Recent research fine-tunes LLMs to generate tests for specified focal methods [39, 41, 63]. For instance, AthenaTest [63] fine-tuned BART [39] to generate tests where the input contains the focal method and its associated code context. The output is the complete test. Nie et al. [41] fine-tuned CodeT5 [65] to generate tests. Chen et al. [7] proposed a novel LLM-based test generation model named ChatU- niTest, which integrates an adaptive focal context mechanism and a generation-validation-repair pipeline. ChatUniTest addresses the limitations of LLM-based tools by optimizing input context and validating test outputs through syntactic, compile-time, and runtime checks. Evaluation against tools like EvoSuite [19] and TestSpark [61] demonstrates ChatUniTest’s superior coverage and reliability across diverse Java projects, highlighting its potential for advancing automated unit test generation. Dakhel et al. [13] introduced MuTAP, a unit test generation framework based on LLMs, which incorporates mutation testing to improve the bug detection capabilities of test cases. MuTAP enhances prompts by including information on surviving mutants, highlighting deficiencies in generated tests, and iteratively optimizing them to produce efficient test cases. Experiments show that MuTAP significantly outperforms existing tools, such as Pynguin [38], in detecting real and synthetic buggy code, particularly in mutation score and fault detection coverage. Given that these models are trained on extensive developer-written code corpora, learning-based approaches can generate tests that closely resemble human-written code [63], highlighting the potential of LLMs ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology, Vol. 35, No. 4, Article 92. Unlike the above work, which directly takes focal methods as input, we adopt CoT prompts as contextual information and combine the focal method with CoT prompts as input to fine-tune LLMs. RL for Code Generation. RL strategies have made significant progress in code generation [35, 53, 59, 69, 75]. For example, Ranzato et al. [53] adopted BLEU [48] and ROUGE [34] as reward scores to optimize DL models and generate codes. Le et al. [31] proposed a novel framework named CodeRL for program synthesis. CodeRL adopts one LLM as the policy model. The reward model is trained to evaluate the correctness of the generated programs and offer feedback to the policy model. Shojaee et al. [59] proposed merging LLMs with PPO for code generation, which is named PPOCoder. PPOCoder leverages non-differentiable feedback from code execution to generate code. Zhang et al. [75] presented LearnedSQLGen, an RL-based SQL generation framework. LearnedSQLGen uses an exploration-exploitation strategy, leveraging feedback from query execution to guide the code generation.Liuetal.[ 35]proposedRLTF,whichleveragestheresultsofunittestsasfeedbacksignals to enhance the overall performance of the model. By incorporating fine-grained unit test feedback, RLTF ensures that the synthesized programs are functionally accurate and optimized for specific application requirements. These techniques exploit feedback from non-differentiable indicators pertinent to specific tasks. Although RL achieved excellent performance in code generation, these studies did not use the code coverage information as the reward score to optimize test generation in existing LLM. Our approach employs line coverage as the reward score and adopts a fine-tuned LLM to predict the line coverage without executing code snippets. 7 Conclusion and Future Work We propose a novel approach that utilizes the CoT prompt and RL strategy to generate unit tests, named TestCTRL. TestCTRL adopts the CoT prompt to fine-tune one LLM (i.e., CodeLlama [56]) as the policy model. Then, TestCTRL utilizes another LLM (i.e., CodeGPT [9, 37]) fine-tuned based on the line coverage as the reward model. Further, TestCTRL employs the PPO algorithm [58] to optimize the policy model. Compared to existing LLM-based test generation approaches, TestCTRLcangeneratemorediverseandrelevanttests.OurexperimentsdemonstratethatTestCTRL consistently improves the performances of test generation on the Defects4J benchmark. In future work, we plan to create a larger dataset that includes more other programming languages and CoT prompts. We also plan to apply the idea of the CoT prompt to other tasks in software engineering, such as automatic patch repair and code summarization. To further validate the generalizability and robustness of TestCTRL, we plan to evaluate our approach in other benchmarks, such as EvoSuite SF110 [19] and BugsInPy [68]. text: PRIMG : Efficient LLM-driven Test Generation Using Mutant Prioritization Mohamed Salah Bouafif Polytechnique Montréal Montréal, Canada mohamed-salah.bouafif@polymtl.ca Mohammad Hamdaqa Polytechnique Montréal Montréal, Canada mhamdaqa@polymtl.ca Edward Zulkoski Quantstamp California, USA ed@quantstamp.com Abstract Mutation testing is a widely recognized technique for assessing and enhancing the effectiveness of software test suites by introducing deliberate code mutations. However, its application often results in overly large test suites, as developers generate numerous tests to kill specific mutants, increasing computational overhead. This paper introduces PRIMG (Prioritization and Refinement Integrated Mutation-driven Generation), a novel framework for incremen- tal and adaptive test case generation for Solidity smart contracts. PRIMG integrates two core components: a mutation prioritization module, which employs a machine learning model trained on mu- tant subsumption graphs to predict the usefulness of surviving mutants, and a test case generation module, which utilizes Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate and iteratively refine test cases to achieve syntactic and behavioral correctness. We evaluated PRIMG on real-world Solidity projects from Code4Arena to assess its effectiveness in improving mutation scores and generating high-quality test cases. The experimental results demonstrate that PRIMG significantly reduces test suite size while maintaining high mutation coverage. The prioritization module consistently outperformed random mutant selection, enabling the generation of high-impact tests with reduced computational effort. Furthermore, the refining process enhanced the correctness and utility of LLM-generated tests, addressing their inherent limitations in handling edge cases and complex program logic. ACM ISBN 979-8-4007-1385-9/25/06 https://doi.org/10.1145/3756681.3756991 1 Introduction Software testing is a critical component of the software develop- ment lifecycle, aimed at ensuring the quality and reliability of soft- ware systems. As systems grow in complexity, the need for effective and efficient testing strategies becomes increasingly paramount. One of the primary challenges in developing efficient test suites is achieving comprehensive coverage while minimizing redundancy. As software systems become more complex, the number of possible execution paths and scenarios increases exponentially. This makes it difficult to create test cases that adequately cover all aspects of the system without becoming unwieldy or time-consuming to exe- cute [21]. To address these challenges, researchers and practitioners have turned to advanced techniques such as search-based software testing (SBST) and heuristic approaches. SBST applies optimization algorithms, such as genetic algorithms, to automatically gener- ate test cases that maximize coverage and fault detection while minimizing the overall size of the test suite. These techniques can explore vast search spaces more efficiently than manual approaches, potentially uncovering edge cases and vulnerabilities that might otherwise be missed. While such approaches have proven their effi- ciency in generating test cases that uncover edge cases, they require significant computational resources, especially for large and com- plex systems. In recent years, mutation testing (MT) has emerged as a powerful technique for assessing and improving the quality of test suites while also guiding the generation of high-quality test cases for the program under test (PUT). Mutation testing is a soft- ware testing technique that involves modifying a program’s source code to create faulty versions, known as mutants, to evaluate the effectiveness of a test suite in detecting errors. While the primary goal of mutation testing is to assess the quality of a test suite by determining whether it can identify and kill mutants, thereby en- suring the reliability and robustness of the software and unveiling edge cases, different approaches have been exploring the usage of surviving mutants to guide the generation of new test cases [28][8]. Generating an adequate test suite using mutation testing can be computationally expensive and time-consuming due to the vast number of possible mutants. Furthermore, using mutants as test goals can lead to an exponential increase in the size of the test suite since each mutant will be killed by a test, and thus running the test suite can become impractical for complex codebases. Liu et al. introduced AID [19], a method combining LLMs with differential testing to generate fault-revealing test cases for programs that have already passed traditional test suites. This approach demonstrates the potential of integrating advanced AI techniques with mutation testing to improve test case generation. However, the generation of valid and effective test cases remains a challenge. The authors in [27] highlighted issues with correctness in LLM-generated test 1107 EASE ’25, June 17–20, 2025, Istanbul, Turkiye Bouafif et al. cases, while Yuan et al. proposed ChatTester[30], an approach that refines test cases iteratively to improve their quality. These studies underscore the need for sophisticated validation and refinement techniques when using AI-generated test cases. While significant efforts have explored the use of Large Lan- guage Models (LLMs) for test case generation, several challenges have emerged, primarily related to ensuring the correctness of the generated tests and the computational intensity required to con- struct high-coverage test suites. Mutation testing aims to improve test quality and coverage by guiding developers to create tests tar- geting surviving mutants. These surviving mutants serve as test goals, with the objective of enhancing code coverage and identify- ing hidden vulnerabilities. However, as the complexity of software systems grows, the number of generated mutants increases expo- nentially, leading to scalability challenges in the process of test generation. Specifically, generating and validating test cases to kill a large number of mutants becomes a computationally expensive and time-consuming process, even when employing LLMs, which require additional resources for iterative refinement. Despite these scalability concerns, the state-of-the-art mutant selection technique remains random selection, which often fails to optimize computa- tional efforts and test effectiveness [9, 17]. In this paper, we introduce PRIMG (Prioritization and Refine- ment Integrated Mutation-driven Generation), a novel approach tailored for incremental test suite generation. PRIMG leverages mu- tation testing to guide the effective use of LLMs in generating and refining test cases for Solidity smart contracts. Our approach aims to achieve effective test generation that optimizes the total number of generated tests while simultaneously enhancing the mutation score. Our proposed technique, employs two main components: a mutation prioritization module, responsible for selecting mu- tants as test goals for the generated test cases, and a test case generation module, which employs an LLM for generating and refining the test cases. The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 briefly reviews the related works. Section 3 describes the different modules of our approach. We present our experimental setup, research ques- tions, and experimental results in Section 4. We discuss our findings in Section 5. Threats to the validity of our results are reviewed in Section 6. Finally, we conclude the paper in Section 7, highlighting some avenues for future work. 2 Related Works The proliferation of smart contracts has established them as a cor- nerstone of automation and trust, facilitating secure and transparent transactions across diverse industries, including finance, real es- tate, and supply chain management [5]. However, their increasing adoption has unveiled numerous challenges. The immutable and transparent nature of smart contracts paradoxically renders them susceptible to exploitation, misuse, and unforeseen vulnerabilities [33]. Consequently, the imperative to conduct rigorous audits of smart contracts arises, entailing a meticulous examination of their code and features to detect and mitigate potential risks[ 33]. The immutable nature of smart contracts adds a new layer of impor- tance for developers and enhances the need for the development of a comprehensive and complete test suite [10]. Over the years, various tools have been developed to automate the task of test case generation for smart contracts. Numerous studies have explored the use of genetic algorithms for test case generation [7, 13]. For example, the authors of [23] investigated the application of meta-heuristic algorithms, implementing multiple search techniques such as random search and genetic algorithms (e.g., NSGAII[23], MOSA[23], and DynaMOSA[ 25]) for effective test case generation. While these approaches have demonstrated promising results, the genetic algorithm approach remains compu- tationally expensive. As highlighted in the in-depth study by Zou et al. [34], generat- ing test suites for smart contracts is a complex task, with several challenges arising throughout their development and implemen- tation. Among the surveyed developers, 54.7% reported the lack of mature and business-ready tools for blockchain-specific devel- opment. Additionally, these tools fail to address all corner cases and scenarios, which is the most critical challenge identified by the developers. The emergence of large language models (LLMs) for software development tasks [12] has sparked interest in leveraging these models for test case generation [24]. Several tools and techniques have been proposed in this area. For example, Arghavan Moradi Dakhela et al. [4] suggested using mutation testing to guide LLMs in generating effective test cases. After an initial mutation campaign, their approach prompts the LLM with surviving mutants, request- ing the generation of tests to kill the mutants. While their empirical evaluation showed promising results, the approach has yet to be tested on large datasets and real-world projects. Large codebases introduce three significant challenges: (1) the large number of gener- ated mutants makes performing mutation testing computationally expensive and time-consuming, (2) the large number of tests re- quired to achieve a high mutation score, and (3) real-world project requires intricate test setups and environments and more complex test case then simple assert-statement tests. 3 Approach In this section, we discuss the different steps of our approach. Figure 1 shows an overview of our proposed approach, and Algorithm 1 presents the sequence of its different steps. PRIMG is composed of two main modules: testcase generation module and mutants prioritization module. We discuss each of the two modules in the following subsections. 3.1 Test Case Generation Module Approach overview: This section details the process of generating test cases as outlined in Algorithm 1. Following an initial mutation testing phase, we identify and select the surviving mutants. The primary objective of the proposed approach is to develop unit tests capable of eliminating the maximum number of these surviving mutants. The process begins by selecting a specific mutant as the testing target, with the selection mechanism described in Section 3.2. The prioritized mutant is then used to generate an initial prompt for the large language model (LLM). Subsequently, the process enters a refinement phase, designed to ensure the correctness of the generated test cases, as elaborated in subsequent sections. If a test case is deemed correct, it is incorporated into the final test suite. 1108 PRIMG : Efficient LLM-driven Test Generation Using Mutant Prioritization EASE ’25, June 17–20, 2025, Istanbul, Turkiye PUT Initial test suite Survived mutants LLM Initial prompt YES NoNO Verify behaviorVerify syntax Augmented prompt Refining process Final test suite YES Survived mutants? NO Generated tests Generate mutants Prompt designProcess Test caseMutant db Prioritization Module Mutation testing Testcase Generation Module Figure 1: The proposed approach for generating a test case using LLMs. Algorithm 1 PRIMG Input: PUT, initialTestSuite, survivingMutants Output: finalTestSuite 1: prioritizedMutant← PrioritizeMutant(survivingMutants) 2: initTest← SelectTest(prioritizedMutant, initialTestSuite) 3: initPrompt← CONCAT(initTest, prioritizedMutant, PUT ) 4: rawIUT← LLM(initPrompt) 5: FUT, success← RefiningTest(rawIUT, PUT, prioritizedMutant) 6: if sucess then 7: Add FUT to finalTestSuite 8: end if 9: return finalTestSuite Conversely, if the refinement process fails to produce a correct test case, the task is classified as problematic or one for which PRIMG is unable to generate an appropriate test case. 3.1.1 Initial Prompt. Large Language Models (LLMs) are adept at performing tasks they have been trained on. However, fine-tuning LLMs to adapt to a new task is computationally expensive. Addition- ally, certain LLMs, such as Codex[3], excel in generating code but are closed-source, making fine-tuning for custom tasks infeasible. Prompt-based learning [20, 31] offers an effective alternative for adapting LLMs to new tasks. A prompt is a combination of natural language and/or programming language context used as input to LLMs. Studies have demonstrated that incorporating natural lan- guage instructions as hints within prompts significantly enhances the ability of LLMs to perform novel tasks [22] . In our approach, the initial prompt consists of three key compo- nents: Algorithm 2 RefiningTest Input: rawIUT, PUT, prioritizedMutant Output: FUT, error 1: correctTest← false 2: FUT← rawIUT 3: counter← 0 4: while not correctTest and counter < loopSize do 5: syntaxVerif, errorSyntax← Compile(FUT ) 6: behaviorVerif, errorBehavior← RunTest(FUT, PUT ) 7: if syntaxVerif and behaviorVerif then 8: correctTest← true 9: else 10: augmentedPrompt← CONCAT(FUT, PUT, errorSyntax, errorBehavior, prioritizedMutant) 11: FUT← LLM(augmentedPrompt) 12: counter← counter + 1 13: end if 14: end while 15: return FUT, correctTest • The Program Under Test (PUT): This represents the orig- inal program prior to mutation. • The Mutant Code: This introduces modifications to the original program, representing potential faults or variations. • An Initial Test File: This file is designed to validate the functionality and setup of the PUT within the testing frame- work. The test file is selected based on the following criteria: (1) The test file should test functions defined in the PUT. This ensures the large language model (LLM) receives suffi- cient information about the testing environment and the imported libraries required to execute the tests. 1109 EASE ’25, June 17–20, 2025, Istanbul, Turkiye Bouafif et al. (2) The test file should contain diverse test cases. This en- hances the LLM’s understanding of the structure and vari- ety of test cases, aiding in the generation of comprehensive and accurate tests. 3.1.2 Refining Process. As illustrated in Algorithm 2, after generat- ing the raw Initial Unit Test (IUT), we employ a refining process to enhance its quality and effectiveness. The refining process consists of two primary steps: Syntax Verifier and Behavior Verifier. In this step, we verify the correctness of the generated test case in two stages: (1) Syntax Verification: The test case is compiled, and logs are reviewed for syntax errors. (2) Behavior Verification: The test case is executed against the PUT. A valid test case must successfully pass when run on the PUT. Prompt Augmentation. If the previous step fails (e.g., the test case fails to compile or the PUT fails when tested), we proceed to prompt augmentation. In this step: • A new prompt is constructed using the PUT, the mutant code, the FUT, and the error logs from the previous step. • This enhanced prompt is used to generate a refined test case, referred to as the Final Unit Test (FUT), which resolves the issues encountered in the initial iteration. By iteratively refining and augmenting the prompt, we ensure the generation of high-quality test cases capable of validating both the syntax and behavior of the program under test. 3.2 Prioritization module 3.2.1 Dynamic Mutant Subsumption Graph. In mutation testing, a test set𝑇 is considered mutation-adequate with respect to a mutant set𝑀 if for every non-equivalent mutant 𝑚𝑖∈ 𝑀, there exists a test𝑡∈𝑇 such that𝑡 detects𝑚𝑖[16]. However, mutation operators generate a significantly larger number of mutants than necessary, leading to redundancy. This redundancy is formally captured by the concept of minimal mutation . A dominator set 𝐷 ⊆ 𝑀 is a minimal subset of𝑀 such that any test set adequate for𝐷 is also adequate for𝑀. A key aspect of mutation testing is thesubsumption relationship between mutants. Given a finite set of mutants𝑀 and a finite test set𝑇 , a mutant𝑚𝑖 is said to dynamically subsume another mutant𝑚 𝑗 if a test𝑡∈𝑇 detects𝑚𝑖 and every test that detects𝑚𝑖 also detects𝑚 𝑗 . This relationship is strict if𝑚𝑖 subsumes𝑚 𝑗 , but 𝑚 𝑗 does not subsume𝑚𝑖. If two mutants𝑚𝑖 and𝑚 𝑗 are detected by exactly the same tests in𝑇 , the subsumption is not strict [15]. The Dynamic Mutant Subsumption Graph (DMSG) captures these sub- sumption relationships. In a DMSG, each node represents a maximal set of redundant mutants, and edges represent the subsumption relationships between sets. Specifically, if mutant𝑚𝑖 strictly sub- sumes mutant𝑚 𝑗 , there is a directed edge from the node containing 𝑚𝑖 to the node containing 𝑚 𝑗 . Any test that detects a mutant in the DMSG is guaranteed to detect all mutants subsumed by that mutant, including those in the same node or lower in the graph. This structure provides an efficient way to identify and eliminate redundant mutants, thereby improving the mutation testing process and reducing the computational burden on developers. 3.2.2 Test Completeness Advancement Probability, TCAP. Test Com- pleteness Advancement Probability (TCAP), as defined in [15], is employed to measure mutant usefulness in the context of test case generation. This measure quantifies the likelihood of a mutant, when presented as a test goal to a developer, eliciting a test case that enhances test completeness by killing the mutant and a maxi- mum number of other mutants. This capture a key idea: a mutant is useful to be selected as the test goal, if when developing a test case that kills that mutant, other mutants are going to be killed by the same developed test case. This is due to the fact that the subsumed mutant,𝑚 𝑗 is killed by the same tests that kills the dominant mu- tant𝑚𝑖. In a subsumption relationship, The test case that kills the dominant mutant are also killing the subsumed mutant. As discussed in [ 15], we define the usefulness of a mutant in terms of its capacity to detect (or kill) other mutants when it is itself killed. However, for surviving mutants (mutants not killed by the initial test suite), it is not feasible to construct a Dominance Mutation Subsumption Graph (DMSG). Instead, TCAP exploits the structural information of the DMSGs of killed mutants. By analyzing these graphs, we can identify mutants that are likely to be useful as test goals. The intuition is that the test suite developed to kill these selected mutants will also effectively kill other mutants, thereby improving the overall efficiency of the test generation process and optimization the total number of needed tests. This approach builds on foundational ideas of mutation analysis and mutant subsumption as explored in prior research [14, 16]. By leveraging the dominance relationships and subsumption hierarchies among mutants, we aim to streamline the test case generation process, improving both coverage and effectiveness throw the usage of a supervised machine learning model. The usefulness factor of a mutant is defined as measurement of its ability to reveal additional mutants when used as a target for test case generation. The usefulness factor of a mutant has two properties: • Dominator mutants, have usefulness factor equal to 1: By definition, each test that kills a dominator mutants kills every other subsumed mutant. • Subsumed mutants, have a usefulness factor less then 1 and greater then 0 3.2.3 Machine learning module. • context feature: Building upon the modeling approach and the feature set proposed by Samuel J. Kaufman et al. [ 15], we incorporated program context features extracted from a program’s Abstract Syntax Tree (AST). For a given mu- tated AST node, we examined its syntactic context, including parent and child nodes within the AST as well as nesting details, and its semantic context, such as the data types of ex- pressions, operands, and method parameters. It is important to highlight that previous studies[32] utilized information derived from test execution data, such as code coverage, to make predictions in the context of mutation analysis. As done in [15], our approach aims to identify mutants that are beneficial for generating test cases that have not yet been created, aligning with the goals of mutation testing. 1110 PRIMG : Efficient LLM-driven Test Generation Using Mutant Prioritization EASE ’25, June 17–20, 2025, Istanbul, Turkiye PUT Mutants DBMutation testing Dominance probability extraction Mutant detection matrix Subsumption graph Dominant mutants Dominant tests Context feature extraction AST creation Mutated node extraction Mutants db Context Feature Extraction Context feature extraction Model training Model infererence db process Labeled dataset Usefulness factor predictions Figure 2: Overview of the dataset labeling process • Feature extraction and dataset labeling : Figure 2 shows an overview of our dataset labeling approach and model training. Since we can only construct the DMSG for the killed mutants, only the killed mutant will be used for training the model. After an initial mutation testing campaign using the initial test suite of the PUT, we create our labeled dataset. The label- ing of the dataset is composed of two modules: Dominance probability extraction and Context feature extraction. The first component is the dominance probability extraction com- ponents which aims to label the killed mutants with an initial usefulness factor. Given the mutation testing results, we cre- ate the mutation matrix which maps test cases to mutants, indicating which test cases can detect (kill) or not specific mu- tants. We use the mutation matrix to construct the DMSG of mutants relative to the initial test suite as defined in the pre- vious section. We extract the parent node which contains the dominant mutants. Those identified dominant mutants are la- beled as useful having the useful factor equal to 1. The other mutants are labeled as having a useful factor equal to zero. The second component is context feature extraction module which aims to extract the context features from the Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) described in the previous section. First we start by comparing the AST of the mutant with the one of the PUT. We identify the mutated node. Using the mutated node we extract the remaining context features of the mutated node and its parent node context features. using the usefulness factor and the context features, we create the labeled dataset that will be used for training and inference. • Machine learning models: We evaluated a small number of model design choices and training settings against an intrinsic measure of model performance with the ultimate goal of choosing a single model for downstream evaluation. Each training setting was a kind of hold-one-out train-test split, using each held out project (or smart contract in a given project) at a time as the evaluation set. We trained all models using Scikit-Learn [ 26] and evaluated every combination of the following choices: We have chosen these configuration: – Model choice : We compared ridge regression to a random forest regression (max depth of 3 and 10 trees). [15, 18] . – features set : We used a comprehensive set of features (All features, enumerated in [14]) – Training Setting : We evaluated the following train-test splits: ∗ All Projects : training on mutants from all projects, including those in non-held-out smart contracts in the same project, and testing on mutants in the held-out smart contracts; ∗ Project-Only: training on mutants in all but one held-out smart contract in a single project and testing on mutants in the held-out smart contract . Building on findings in [15], we choose the following configura- tion for the experiments in the evaluation section: Model=Linear, Features=All, Training Setting=Project-Only 4 Evaluation In this section, we describe the evaluations we designed and con- ducted to investigate the following research questions. (1) RQ1. How efficient is the pipeline for test case genera- tion? (2) RQ2. How useful is the prioritization technique com- pared to random for efficient mutation testing? 4.1 Experimental Setup In this section, we present our experiment setup. Specifically, we describe the mutant generation tool, clarify the LLM of PRIMG and its setup, and indicate the benchmark data sets used in our 1111 EASE ’25, June 17–20, 2025, Istanbul, Turkiye Bouafif et al. experiments. We conducted the experiment on an EC2 instance of type g5.xlarge with 26 GiB of GPU memory. 4.1.1 Experiment Parameters. We call the refining process on the LLM up to 10 times and collect the output that meets two criteria: The generated test must compile correctly and then pass the PUT. If after 10 runs, the LLM is not able to generate an output that satisfies these two conditions, we consider the mutant as a problematic task or a task for which PRIMG is not able to generate a test case. For the prioritization module, for each project we train a machine learning model to predict the survived mutant usefulness factor. As mentioned in section 3.2.3, we use the configuration of: Linear model with all features. As we have already explained, the model is trained on mutants that have already been killed. We use llama 3.1 as the large language model for the generation of test case and refinement of test cases. 4.1.2 Mutant Generator. To apply mutation testing, we need to generate different mutant versions of a PUT by modifying different lines of code to introduce vulnerabilities. For this purpose we use SuMo [1] as mutant generation tool. SuMo is a mutation testing tool adapted for smart contracts of Solidity. It uses different muta- tion operators to generate mutants including 25 Solidity-specific operators and 19 general-purpose mutation operators. For testing, we used Ganache1 as a local blockchain network for testing and deploying smart contracts and executing transactions for mutants and PUT. We use hardhat as testing framework 2. 4.1.3 Data sources. To conduct our experiments, we chose real world projects that we extracted from code4arena 3. Code4arena is a platform facilitating decentralized security audits of smart contracts through competitive audit contests conducted by a global community of security researchers. We selected three different projects. The details of the selected project is in the following Table 1. To ensue rigor, we chose projects meeting these specific criteria: • Number of smart contracts: this criterion ensures the selec- tion of complex projects by focusing on those with more than 10 smart contracts, avoiding overly straightforward examples. • Initial test suite: in the selected project, the initial test suite must have at least one test case testing each smart contract. • Mutation score: projects are chosen with an initial mutation score (MS) below 80%, ensuring that the existing test suite is insufficient and requires additional test cases to improve coverage. All scripts and dataset can be found here 4. 4.2 Empirical Study Results This section discusses our findings for each research question (RQ), focusing on the performance and efficiency of the proposed ap- proaches. 1Truffle Suite, Ganache - One Click Blockchain , https://trufflesuite.com/ganache/, ac- cessed on Nov 26, 2024. 2Hardhat, https://hardhat.org/, accessed on Nov 26, 2024. 3https://code4rena.com 4https://github.com/Salah-SH/llm-mutation-testing 4.2.1 Evaluation of the Performance of the Test Case Gener- ation Module. In this subsection, we target to answer the first research question. We divide the RQ1 to two sub questions and answer each one of them presenting our findings. RQ1. How efficient is the pipeline for test case generation? In this research question, we evaluate the performance of the test case generation module with respect to two key aspects: (1) the effectiveness of refining module in generating correct test cases and (2) the ability of these generated tests to kill new mutants that were not initially addressed by the original test suite. To en- sure a comprehensive analysis, RQ1 is divided into the following subquestions: • RQ1.1: How efficient is the pipeline for generating syntacti- cally and behaviorally correct tests? The objective here is to assess the accuracy of the test cases generated by the LLM. Correctness is evaluated on two di- mensions: syntactic correctness: The test case compiles successfully, and behavioral correctness: The test case passes the original Program Under Test (PUT) without er- rors. • RQ1.2: What is the impact of the size of the refining loop on the correctness of the generated tests? This sub-question investigates how the number of iterations in the refining loop impacts the quality of the generated test cases. Specifically, it examines whether iterative improve- ments significantly enhance the syntactic and behavioral correctness of the test cases. To answer RQ1.1, test cases were generated by prompting the LLM with and without the refining process using different loop sizes. A test case is considered correct if it successfully compiles and passes the original PUTs. The results were collected from three projects, as listed in Table 1. To answer RQ1.1 and statistically evaluate the impact of the refining process, we formulated the following hypotheses [29]: RQ1.1-H0: The refining process does not significantly improve the number of correct tests compared to a single-shot prompt. RQ1.1-H1: The refining process significantly improves the number of correct tests compared to a single-shot prompt. To evaluate the efficiency of the test generation process, we analyzed the performance of test case generation with respect to the number of correctly generated test cases across varying trial counts. Table 3 summarizes the results obtained when running the process with 1 trial, 5 trials, and 10 trials. To assess the statistical significance of the differences between these configurations, we performed pairwise Z-tests for proportions, a statistical method suitable for comparing success rates across independent trials. The comparisons were conducted across three projects: Allobase, Particle, and Quadrata. The results of the Z-tests for each project are as follows: • Allobase: Significant differences were observed between 1 trial and 5 trials (𝑍 =−19.08,𝑝 < 0.05) as well as 1 trial and 10 trials (𝑍 =−19.20,𝑝 < 0.05). No significant difference was found between 5 trials and 10 trials (𝑍 =−0.22,𝑝 > 0.05). 1112 PRIMG : Efficient LLM-driven Test Generation Using Mutant Prioritization EASE ’25, June 17–20, 2025, Istanbul, Turkiye Table 1: Data sources Project Id # smart contracts # initial test files Initial mutation score % Allobase 31 12 35.89 Particle 19 7 46.86 Quadrata 10 9 77 Figure 3: Number of test cases by trial and projects • Particle: Significant differences were observed between 1 trial and 5 trials (𝑍 =−12.13,𝑝 < 0.05) and 1 trial and 10 trials (𝑍 =−12.13,𝑝 < 0.05). No significant difference was found between 5 trials and 10 trials (𝑍 = 0.0,𝑝 = 1.0). • Quadrata: Significant differences were observed between 1 trial and 5 trials (𝑍 =−10.24,𝑝 < 0.05) and 1 trial and 10 trials (𝑍 =−10.54,𝑝 < 0.05). No significant difference was found between 5 trials and 10 trials (𝑍 =−0.35,𝑝 = 0.73). Project Single Shot Refining process loop of 5 Refining process loop of 10 Allobase 23/500 201/500 203/500 Particle 10/500 151/500 151/500 Quadrata 21/500 140/500 145/500 Table 2: Number of correct test case generated in different Projects using different loop size Specifically, for the projects Allobase, Particle, and Quadrata, the Z-test results provide strong evidence that increasing the number of trials significantly enhances the success rates of generating correct tests. These findings suggest that using more trials contributes to better test generation performance, as evidenced by the statistically significant improvements observed when increasing from 1 trial to 5 trials and from 1 trial to 10 trials. However, no significant differences were found between 5 and 10 trials across all projects, indicating diminishing returns beyond 5 trials. The observed differences in success rates are statistically significant under the experimental conditions and datasets analyzed. Thus, increasing the number of trials, particularly from 1 to 5, outperforms single-shot attempts in generating correct tests, highlighting the value of incorporating multiple trials in improving LLM-generated test cases. Additionally, as shown in Table 2, the impact of the refining process on the performance of test case generation is evident. In the Allobase project, the single-shot approach generates only 4.6% of correct tests, whereas using the refining process with a loop size of 5 iterations results in a substantial improvement, with 40.2% of tests being correct. Similarly, for theParticle project, the single-shot approach yields only 2% correct tests, while applying the refining process with 5 iterations increases the correct tests to 30.2%. In the case of Quadrata, the single-shot approach results in 4.2% correct tests, and refining with 5 iterations improves this to 28%. These results indicate a significant performance boost when employing the refining module, demonstrating that iterative refinement is a crucial factor in improving the accuracy and effectiveness of the test case generation module. Therefore, we conclude that utilizing the refining module greatly enhances the performance of the test case generation process, making it a valuable strategy for generating higher-quality test cases in all evaluated projects. Finding 1: The refining module can significantly improve the correctness of the generated tests. To answer RQ1.2, we conducted an additional analysis focusing on the effect of loop size on the correctness of the generated tests. In this research question, our primary objective is to evaluate the role of the number of iterations (loop size) within the refining module on the overall performance of the test case generation process. The hypothesis guiding this investigation was based on the premise that increasing the number of loops could lead to more refined and accurate test cases. The results of this analysis, including detailed performance comparisons for each project, are presented in Table 2. We formulated the null hypothesis (H0) and alternative hypoth- esis (H1) to test the impact of the number of trials as follows: RQ1.2-H0: Both 5 and 10 loops significantly improve the number of correct test cases compared to single-shot for all projects. RQ1.2-H1: Increasing the number of trials in the test generation process positively impacts the success rate of generated test cases. To analyze the performance of the test generation module across different trial configurations (1 trial, 5 trials, and 10 trials), we employed pairwise Z-tests for proportions. These tests compare the success rates of correctly generated tests for different numbers of trials. The Z-test was applied to all three projects, Allobase, Particle, and Quadrata, and the results are summarized below: • Allobase: No significant difference was found between 5 and 10 trials (𝑍 =−0.22,𝑝 > 0.05). • Particle: No significant difference was found between 5 and 10 trials (𝑍 = 0.00,𝑝 > 0.05). 1113 EASE ’25, June 17–20, 2025, Istanbul, Turkiye Bouafif et al. • Quadrata: No significant difference was found between 5 and 10 trials (𝑍 =−0.35,𝑝 > 0.05). These findings suggest that increasing the number of trials from 1 to 5 significantly improves the success rates of test case generation across all projects. However, further increases beyond 5 trials do not result in statistically significant improvements. The Z-test results emphasize the value of employing multiple trials, particularly up to 5, to enhance the accuracy and reliability of LLM-generated test cases. Finding 2: No significant improvement is observed when in- creasing from 5 to 10 loops, suggesting diminishing returns beyond 5 iterations. Overall, the results suggest that the the refining loop technique using a loop size of 5 is the best configuration for optimal test case generation performance. 4.2.2 Evaluation of the performance of prioritization mod- ule. In this subsection, we target the second research question investigating the impact and the effectiveness of the prioritization module for improving the efficiency of the generated tests. RQ2. How useful is the prioritization technique compared to random for efficient mutation testing? To evaluate the prioritization module, we perform analysis on the tests generated for the projects as mentioned in Section ??. For each project among the three projects, we generated 500 tests using the test case generation module. We train a linear model for each project as described in Section 3.2. We use the configuration Model=Linear, Features=all, Training Setting=Project-Only. We distinguish between 2 types of tests: (1) Prioritized test is a test case that have been generated targeting a prioritized mutant and (2) random test is test that has been generated targeting a random mutant. In Table ?? we illustrate the results of the mutation testing we executed using three random set of tests composed of 50 tests and one prioritized set of tests. To answer RQ2, we conducted a hypoth- esis test on the results project Allobase, Particle and Quadrata as presented in Table ??. We formulated the null hypothesis (H0) and the alternative hypothesis (H1) as follows: RQ2-H0: There is no statistically significant difference in the perfor- mance of prioritized generated tests compared to randomly generated tests RQ2-H1: There is a statistically significant difference in the perfor- mance of prioritized generated tests compared to randomly generated tests Similar to RQ1.1 and RQ1.2, we compare the efficacy of these strategies (i.e., prioritized tests vs. randomly selected tests) by using Z-test. • Allobase: The Z-test for this comparison yielded 𝑍 = −15.98,𝑝 < 0.05, indicating a statistically significant dif- ference between the two methods, with Method 2 outper- forming Method 1. • Particle: The Z-test for this comparison yielded 𝑍 = −12.94,𝑝 < 0.05, also showing a statistically significant dif- ference between the two methods, with Method 2 performing better than Method 1. • Quadrata: The Z-test for this comparison yielded 𝑍 = −14.12,𝑝 < 0.05, demonstrating a statistically significant difference between the two methods, with Method B outper- forming Method A. These results suggest that, across all three projects, Allobase, Particle, and Quadrata, the test suite composed of prioritized tests significantly outperforms the test suite composed of random tests set generated using random selection of mutants in killing mutants. The observed differences in success rates are statistically signif- icant under the experimental conditions analyzed, highlighting the effectiveness of the prioritization technique in killing mutants. Thus, the prioritization module consistently enhances test perfor- mance, demonstrating its superiority over random selection in all the evaluated projects. These results highlight the potential of the prioritization strategy as a valuable tool in mutation testing, con- tributing to more efficient and targeted test generation in software testing practices. Finding 3: There is a statistically significant difference in the performance of prioritized generated tests compared to randomly generated tests in killing mutants. 5 Discussions 5.1 Interpretation of the importance of the loop size on the effectiveness of test case generation Although the refining module have shown impressive results in generating and refining generated tests, experiments in the eval- uation section shows that increasing the size of the loop does not considerably improve the number of correctly generated tests since even having a larger trial number, the LLM still fails to generate cor- rect tests no matter the number of repetitions. In fact, LLMs operate based on statistical patterns in their training data rather than true understanding of programming concepts or software semantics[6]. This can lead to what researchers call "hallucination" - generating plausible-looking but incorrect code that doesn’t actually fix the underlying bug[11]. As Dou et al. observed in their extensive study, functional bugs constitute the highest proportion of errors in LLM- generated code fixes, with misunderstanding and logic errors being particularly prevalent[6]. Even after multiple attempts, an LLM may continue to make similar mistakes if it fundamentally misun- derstands the problem or lacks the specific knowledge needed to generate a correct fix. Besides, the token-by-token generation pro- cess of LLMs can lead to inconsistencies in longer code sequences, even if individual parts seem correct. This is particularly prob- lematic for bug fixes that require changes across multiple lines or functions. The authors in [6] observed that LLMs tend to perform better on localized, single-line fixes but struggle with bugs that require broader context or multiple coordinated changes. Further- more, the limited context window of most LLMs can prevent them 1114 PRIMG : Efficient LLM-driven Test Generation Using Mutant Prioritization EASE ’25, June 17–20, 2025, Istanbul, Turkiye Project Randomly Selected Tests Prioritized Tests Ground Truth 1 2 3 Allobase 200 158 8 300 465 Particle 196 54 180 250 350 Quadrata 55 205 200 256 403 Table 3: Overlaid Table representing the number of killed mutants using Randomly Selected Tests, Prioritized Test, and Ground Truth from fully considering all relevant parts of a large codebase, leading to fixes that may solve one issue but introduce new bugs elsewhere. These structural limitations of LLMs mean that even with repeated attempts, they may struggle to generate consistently correct and comprehensive bug fixes for more complex software issues. 5.2 Adequacy of our approach for practical applications The PRIMG framework presents a practical and efficient solution for test suite generation by integrating automated test case gener- ation with an advanced prioritization module. Leveraging Large Language Models (LLMs), the framework automates the creation of diverse, high-quality test cases, minimizing the manual effort required from developers while ensuring robust coverage of edge cases and complex scenarios. Complementing this, the prioritiza- tion module employs machine learning to rank and focus on the most impactful mutants, optimizing the testing process by reducing redundant efforts and maintaining high mutation coverage with a smaller, more efficient test suite. This dual approach significantly enhances the efficiency of mutation testing, streamlining the tra- ditionally resource-intensive process and enabling developers to concentrate on critical tests. Particularly in domains like smart contract development, where rapid and reliable testing is crucial, PRIMG demonstrates its value by reducing computational over- head and improving the precision and practicality of the testing workflow. Its combination of automation, prioritization, and scala- bility establishes PRIMG as a powerful tool for advancing software quality in both research and industrial contexts. 6 Data Availability All the scripts and results that have been used during our experi- ments can be found in this github repository https://github.com/ Salah-SH/llm-mutation-testing 7 Threat to Validity In this study, we employed two different prompt-based learning techniques: one-shot and prompting augmenting technique. How- ever, we did not explore the potential impact of altering the nat- ural language instructions or demonstrative examples (for the prompt augmenting technique) within our prompts. Modifying these instructions or utilizing different demonstrative examples more closely aligned with the PUT’s functionality could potentially enhance the results. A potential threat to the validity of our study arises from the choice of mutation operators defined within the SuMo framework[2]. Mutation operators play a critical role in gener- ating test cases, and the limited set of operators available in SuMo may not adequately represent all possible vulnerabilities in smart contracts. This can lead to a biased set of mutants, limiting the effectiveness of the generated tests in detecting a broad range of issues. If the operators do not cover diverse attack vectors or edge cases, the results of the mutation testing may not fully reflect the real-world security risks present in smart contracts, potentially compromising the generalize-ability of our findings. Another validity threat arises from the exclusive use of Hardhat as the testing framework. While Hardhat is a widely adopted and robust tool for smart contract development and testing, its exclusive use may restrict the applicability of our results to other testing environments. Variations in how different frameworks execute and interact with smart contracts could lead to discrepancies in test outcomes. As a result, the conclusions drawn from Hardhat-based testing might not extend to projects using alternative frameworks, thus reducing the external validity of our study. Additionally, this study did not evaluate the number of newly killed mutants or the impact of the new tests on the overall mutation score. Although this metric is important, our primary focus was on generating correct and valid test cases. A further threat to validity arises from the practical challenges and resource limitations encountered during testing. While there is no inherent limitation in the availability of projects, the com- plexities involved in setting up the testing environment and the constrained resources for conducting extensive experiments re- stricted the scope of our analysis. 8 Conclusion This paper presented PRIMG (Prioritization and Refinement Integrated Mutation-driven Generation), a novel framework for incremental and adaptive test case generation tailored for Solidity smart contracts. By integrating a mutation prioritization module with a test case generation module leveraging Large Language Mod- els (LLMs), PRIMG addresses key challenges in mutation testing, such as excessive test suite sizes and inefficiencies in test generation. The mutation prioritization module employs machine learning models trained on mutant subsumption graphs to predict the use- fulness of mutants, enabling the selection of high-impact test goals. Simultaneously, the test case generation module iteratively refines LLM-generated tests to ensure syntactic and behavioral correctness. Our evaluation on real-world Solidity projects demonstrated PRIMG’s effectiveness in improving mutation scores while reduc- ing test suite size and computational overhead. The prioritization module consistently outperformed random mutant selection by enabling more efficient and targeted test case generation. Moreover, the refining process successfully mitigated common issues associ- ated with LLM-generated tests, such as syntactic errors and limited bug-detection capabilities. 1115 EASE ’25, June 17–20, 2025, Istanbul, Turkiye Bouafif et al. Although the current version of PRIMG employs mutant pri- oritization and LLMs to generate test cases for Solidity contracts programs, its design and evaluation methodology are fundamentally adaptable to various programming languages and models. There- fore, as future work, it can be easily expanded to encompass other programming languages or incorporate new LLMs. References [1] Morena Barboni, Andrea Morichetta, and Andrea Polini. 2021. text: Benchmarking LLMs for Unit Test Generation from Real-World Functions DONG HUANG,National University of Singapore, Singapore JIE M. ZHANG,King’s College London, London, UK MARK HARMAN,University College London, London, UK QIANRU ZHANG∗, The University of Cambridge, Cambridge, UK MINGZHE DU∗, National University of Singapore, Singapore SEE-KIONG NG,National University of Singapore, Singapore Recently, large language models (LLMs) have shown great promise in automating unit test generation, significantly reducing the manual effort required by developers. To effectively evaluate the capabilities of LLMs in this domain, it is crucial to have a well-designed benchmark that accurately reflects real-world scenarios and mitigates common pitfalls. Existing LLM test generation benchmarks are limited by two critical drawbacks: data contamination and structurally simple function code. As a result, scientific conclusions drawn from empirical studies using these benchmarks may be compromised. The evidence presented may be biased due to contamination and may fail to generalize beyond toy programs due to structural simplicity. To address these problems, we introduce ULT (UnLeakedTestbench), a new benchmark specifically designed for function- level unit test generation from real-world Python functions. ULT is constructed through a multi-stage curation process that ensures high cyclomatic complexity and mitigates test case contamination. With 3,909 carefully selected function- level tasks, ULT provides a more realistic and challenging evaluation of LLMs’ test generation capabilities. We also provide PLT(PreLeakedTestbench),apairbenchmarkofULTwithleakedtestsdesignedtoenableacontrolledanalysisofmemorization versus reasoning in test generation. Based on the two datasets, we conduct a large-scale empirical study involving 12 state-of- the-art LLMs, comparing their performance against established benchmarks. Our evaluation results demonstrate that ULT is significantly more challenging. For example, test cases generated by LLMs only achieve 41.32%, 45.10%, 30.22%, and 40.21% for accuracy, statement coverage, branch coverage, and mutation score on average for all LLMs, respectively. These results are substantially lower than the corresponding metrics on TestEval (91.79%, 92.18%, 82.04%, and 49.69%) and PLT (47.07%, 55.13%, 40.07%, and 50.80%). In addition, different from existing benchmarks, ULT shows a strong correlation between test generation performance and code generation performance. For example, the correlation coefficient between the coding ability and test generation performance (𝑃 𝑎𝑠𝑠@1) on ULT is 0.79 (p = 0.002), while it is only 0.56 (p = 0.059) and 0.52 (p = 0.080) on TestEval and PLT, respectively. This indicates that ULT more effectively measures the generalization ability of LLMs. We also make ULT and evaluation results publicly available to foster further research1. ULT is available at https://github.com/huangd1999/ ∗Both Qianru Zhang and Mingzhe Du are corresponding authors. 1To preserve the integrity of the benchmark and prevent test case leakage into future LLM training sets, we do not release the ground-truth tests. Instead, we provide the complete evaluation results for all models benchmarked in this paper. This allows researchers to compare new models against our findings without compromising the benchmark. CCS Concepts: •Computing methodologies→ Natural language generation; •Software and its engineering→ Software defect analysis. Additional Key Words and Phrases: Large language models, unit test generation 1 Introduction Reliable and robust software systems are essential in today’s technology-driven world, where software failures can lead to significant financial losses, reputational damage, and even safety risks. Effective software testing is the cornerstone of achieving this reliability, serving as a systematic approach to validate that software behaves as intended under various conditions and to identify defects before deployment [1, 2]. Among the various layers of testing, unit testing holds a particularly critical position [3]. Unit testing involves the creation of specific test inputs designed to scrutinize individual components or “units” of software, typically functions, in isolation. The primary objective of unit test generation is to cover diverse program statements and execution branches [4–6], thereby detecting defects early in the development lifecycle when they are least expensive to fix, and facilitating safer code refactoring and maintenance. However, despite its importance, the manual composition of comprehensive unit test suites is usually labor-intensive and intellectually demanding. Existing research and industry experience consistently highlight the significant manual effort, time investment, and domain expertise traditionally required, making it a frequent bottleneck in agile development environments [5, 7, 8]. To address this challenge and accelerate the unit test generation process, recent research has increasingly explored the application of LLMs in automated test case generation [9–17]. With their advanced capabilities in code understanding and generation, LLMs have shown promise in automating aspects of test case generation. However, the quality of LLM-generated tests is also critical; inadequately generated tests may fail to detect crucial bugs, leading to a false sense of security and the propagation of vulnerabilities into production systems. Specifically, we first detail the multi- stage curation process designed to yield a high-quality dataset characterized by real-world relevance, controlled complexity, and mitigated data contamination. Subsequently, we define the distinct task formats through which LLMs are prompted and their test generation capabilities are assessed. Finally, we outline the specific effectiveness metrics used to quantify and compare the performance of LLMs in these tasks. 3.2 Benchmark Construction Data CollectionWe aim to evaluate LLMs’ ability to generate unit tests for real-world Python functions, focusing on their capacity to cover diverse program statements and execution branches. To achieve this, we begin by ACM Trans. Softw. Eng. Methodol. Benchmarking LLMs for Unit Test Generation from Real-World Functions • 7 collecting candidate Python functions from The Stack v2 [25], a large and diverse corpus of permissively licensed source code. The Stack v2 is a vast collection of open-source code, encompassing a wide range of programming languages and domains, making it an ideal source for our benchmark. After collecting the candidate functions, we implement a rigorous multi-stage filtering pipeline to select suitable candidates. The filtering process is designed to ensure that the selected functions are sufficiently complex, self-contained, and free from contamination (for ULT only), by pre-existing test cases. We introduce each step in the following. Filtering by Cyclomatic ComplexityOne of the core aims of our benchmark work is to assess an LLM’s ability to generate test cases for functions with non-trivial control flow, thereby requiring tests that cover code statements and branches. Functions that are overly simplistic (e.g., possessing only a single execution path) do not offer a discerning challenge for this purpose. To address this, we follow the setup of TestEval [5] and employ cyclomatic complexity3 as a quantitative measure of a program’s structural complexity. Cyclomatic complexity measures the number of linearly independent paths through a program’s source code. It acts as a proxy for the logical “difficulty” of a function: a higher value implies the function contains more decision points (such as “if” statements, loops, and exception handlers), making it structurally intricate. We use this metric toensurewearenotevaluatingmodelsontrivialcode,butratheronfunctionsthatrequiresophisticatedreasoning to test comprehensively. Given the control flow graph of a program, its cyclomatic complexity𝑉 is defined as 𝑉 = 𝑒 − 𝑛 + 𝑝 , where 𝑒 is the number of edges,𝑛 is the number of nodes, and𝑝 is the number of connected components in the graph. A higher cyclomatic complexity generally indicates a greater number of decision points and potential execution paths within a function. We filter out functions with a cyclomatic complexity of less than 10. The functions retained in our dataset after all filtering stages possess an average cyclomatic complexity of 14.87, ensuring a substantive level of logical complexity for testing. We acknowledge that the use of cyclomatic complexity can be controversial, with some studies arguing that it often serves as a proxy for code size [36, 37]. However, we do not claim it necessarily represents “conceptual complexity.” Instead, we use it strictly as a structural filter to guarantee the selection of functions with nested Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) structures that characterize complex control flow. Without this filter, we might inadvertently include long methods that lack any significant branching substructure. By enforcing a minimum cyclomatic complexity, we explicitly select for functions that possess non-trivial branching logic. Therefore, we use it as a measure of AST complexity, and since it is also correlated with size, we ensure that as complexity increases, we are evaluating larger programs with meaningful branching. We further validate this assumption by analyzing the correlation between cyclomatic complexity and the performance of LLMs on our test generation tasks (See Section 5.2). Self-Containment For effective unit test generation, it is crucial that the function under test (FUT) can be evaluated in relative isolation, without complex external dependencies that the LLM might lack context for, such as custom functions or classes defined elsewhere in a large project. If a function heavily relies on other custom functions or classes defined elsewhere in a large project, an LLM provided only with the FUT’s source code may struggle to generate correct and executable tests due to missing knowledge of these external components. Therefore, we analyzed the remaining functions to identify and filter out those that exhibited direct dependencies on or interactions with other non-standard, user-defined functions or complex class structures not passed as simple arguments. This step aims to ensure that the context provided to the LLM (primarily the function’s own source code and potentially its signature) is largely sufficient for generating meaningful tests. This design choice aligns with the fundamental principle of unit testing, which seeks to verify internal logic in isolation. By filtering out deep cross-module dependencies, we specifically evaluate the model’s ability to generate logic-covering inputs without the confounding risk of hallucinating external state or dependencies.
