Introduction 1 1 Introduction Software testing is the most critical yet time-consuming phase of the software development lifecycle, covering around 40–60% of the entire project effort or cost in many industrial environments. (Srivastava, 2009). Even with this much effort, it can still be challenging to achieve comprehensive test coverage that identifies real defects. Unit testing, while fundamental to software quality assurance, is often deprioritized under tight deadlines, which leads to undertested code entering production systems (Touré et al, 2017). Recent advancements in automated test generation present promising solutions to this issue. Standard search-based methods, such as Pynguin, use genetic algorithms to systematically explore execution paths, but innovative LLM-based tools like MuTAP utilize the code comprehension abilities of large language models together with mutation testing to generate tests that are more semantically aware. Despite their common goal of automating unit test development, these systems operate on fundamentally different foundations, and their comparative effectiveness, efficiency, and practical application remain unclear. Search-based tools offer controlled and reproducible test generation with predictable resource expenses, as they operate within a user-defined search budget (Arcuri & Briand, 2014). However, they may encounter challenges with complex semantic requirements, particularly in dynamically typed languages like Python, where limited static type information constrains precise input modelling (Lukasczyk & Fraser, 2022). LLM-based approaches promise higher-quality, more readable tests through natural language understanding but introduce concerns about computational costs, reliability, and reproducibility (Pizzorno & Berger, 2025; Chen Y, et al., 2024). Existing evaluations of automated test generation tools generally focus on a single tool in isolation or compare tools within the same framework (Fraser & Arcuri, 2014). There are limited controlled, direct practical comparisons of fundamentally different generation approaches, particularly between search-based and mutation-aware LLM-based systems (Fraser & Arcuri, 2014). This gap limits the ability to make meaningful conclusions about their relative strengths, weaknesses, and suitability for real-world application. The development of production-ready LLM-based testing tools represents a potential shift in automated test generation, as these techniques depend on the semantic reasoning of source code rather than relying solely on traditional search or feedback-driven methods. (Chen, et al., 2021) (Schäfer, et al., 2023). However, there is currently a lack of extensive empirical data comparing LLM-based approaches with well-known search-based tools for companies planning on implementation. This comparison is especially important considering the resource implications. Unlike traditional search-based techniques, which run locally and spend mainly computational costs, LLM-based test generation frequently depends on commercial APIs or resource-intensive models. A further limitation of existing work is, only few studies provide comparisons among different domains, these evaluations are often limited to open-source benchmarks with little work addressing industrial settings (Wang et al, 2018) and focus primarily on structural coverage or mutation score metrics (Fraser Introduction 2 & Arcuri, 2014) (Lukasczyk & Fraser, 2022). Practical factors such as setup complexity, manual intervention, reproducibility, and tool stability are often underreported or not systematically evaluated in empirical studies (Lukasczyk & Fraser, 2022) (Fraser & Arcuri, 2014). Production codebases often differ from public benchmarks. Whether performance patterns found in open-source libraries are replicated in commercial code has not been directly explored in prior comparative studies. This thesis addresses these limitations through a multidimensional empirical comparison of Pynguin and MuTAP on 26 Python modules: 14 from open-source libraries and 12 from an industrial codebase provided under data processing agreements. 25 were included in the full analysis. Prior to analysis, the industrial modules were anonymised by replacing all identifiers with neutral labels and removing references to internal systems and private APIs. Because the original MuTAP implementation transmits source code to OpenAI's Codex API, which is incompatible with the industrial collaborator's data sovereignty requirements, MuTAP was modified to operate locally using Llama 3.1 8B via Ollama. This adaption preserved full pipeline operation while meeting GDPR and IP protection requirements. The comparison includes test quality as measured by mutation score and structural coverage, computational efficiency including execution time and LLM API call counts, domain-specific performance across open-source and industrial subjects and developer experience including setup complexity, failure analysis, manual effort, generated test code structural quality, and compliance requirements. Each factor is evaluated systematically, with the aim of reaching conclusions that reflect the overall cost of implementation rather than just performance measures. The study is structured around four research questions: • How does test quality, measured through mutation testing, compare between search-based and LLM-based generation approaches? • What are the computational efficiency trade-offs in terms of time and resource consumption? • How do these tools perform across different code contexts (open source vs. corporate)? • What is the practical usability experience, including setup complexity and required manual intervention? With these questions answered, this research provides evidence-based guidance for selecting appropriate test generation approaches. They contribute empirical data on the circumstances under which LLM-based mutation-aware testing performs relative to a search-based generation, the limitations of open-source benchmark evaluation as a determinant of industrial performance, and the organizational requirements that determine whether LLM-based tools can be used in regulated environments. Background 3 2 Background 2.1 Automated Test Generation Automated test generation has been a major study area for over two decades, including search-based, model-based, and symbolic execution approaches. The goal of these methods is to reduce the amount of manual labor needed to build and manage test suites. The techniques try to automatically generate input data and test cases that simulate program behavior while meeting certain quality criteria, including structural coverage or fault detection ability (McMinn, 2004) (Harman, et al., 2009). Early automated test generation approaches relied heavily on random testing, which generates inputs without systematic exploration of program structure. The main benefit of random testing is its simplicity and applicability; it requires no software analysis, runs quickly, and can identify unanticipated errors through sheer volume of test executions. Tools such as QuickCheck for Haskell (MacIver, et al., 2019) and Hypothesis for Python (Lackner & Schlingloff, 2012) demonstrate that property-based random testing, where users specify properties that should hold for all inputs, can effectively identify complex errors in functional code. However, when programs contain complex input structures or deeply nested conditional logic, the probability that randomly generated inputs will exercise specific program paths becomes extremely low (Godefroid, et al., 2005). This limitation has been recognized and motivated the development of more guided test generation approaches, such as search-based and symbolic execution techniques (McMinn, 2004; Cadar & Sen, 2013). Search-based software testing (SBST) addresses test generation as a matter related to optimization. Instead of randomly sampling inputs, search-based software testing uses metaheuristic search algorithms, typically genetic algorithms, to iteratively improve test suites according to quality metrics such as structural coverage and fault detection effectiveness (McMinn, 2004; Harman, et al., 2009). Modern search-based software testing tools, such as EvoSuite, which generates JUnit tests, offer full test suite optimization, where the quality metrics are evaluated at the level of the entire test suite rather than individual branches. This approach helps mitigate plateau issues that come with single branch targeting strategies (Fraser & Arcuri, 2014). For the Python ecosystem, Pynguin uses similar strategies adapted to dynamic languages. Pynguin executes the program being tested and iteratively refines test inputs to increase structural coverage. (Lukasczyk & Fraser, 2022). Although search-based software testing tools are powerful for precise structural optimization, they can also be difficult to configure and struggle with complex dependencies, environmental interactions, or dynamic runtime behaviour (Lukasczyk & Fraser, 2022; Fraser & Arcuri, 2014). Another category of automated test generation is symbolic execution, which represents a unique framework. Classical symbolic execution treats program inputs as symbolic variables and executes the program symbolically, using Background 4 path conditions to represent the constraints required to follow each execution path. These path conditions are solved using SMT solvers to generate concrete test inputs that systematically explore new feasible paths (Cadar & Sen, 2013). Tools like KLEE for C/C++ (Cadar, et al., 2008) and Pex (Tillmann & Halleux, 2008) for .NET have demonstrated the power of symbolic execution, achieved high coverage and uncovered subtle bugs in real-world software. However, this approach has serious scalability challenges. The number of possible paths grows rapidly with the number of branches (path explosion), and modern SMT solvers struggle with complex constraints such as strings, floating-point arithmetic, or external library calls (Cadar & Sen, 2013). Therefore, symbolic execution is most effective for testing and analyzing small functions with a manageable path complexity. The progress of large language models (LLMs) trained on large-scale code repositories has opened a new direction for automated test generation. Instead of depending on search or symbolic exploration, these models generate tests by predicting code based on learned patterns from extensive coding libraries. Systems including OpenAI Codex (Chen, et al., 2021) GPT-4, and open-source models such as StarCoder (Li, et al., 2023) have proven exceptional code synthesis abilities. In this situation, test generation represents a translation task rather than an optimization problem, in which prompts in natural language or source code context are transformed directly into executable test cases. One of the main strengths of LLM-based test generation is its ability to understand semantics. These models frequently identify what a unit of code is supposed to accomplish based on information such as function signatures, docstrings, and variable names, and generate tests that show that intended behavior (Chen, et al., 2021; Schäfer, et al., 2023). These test cases closely resemble human-written tests, with descriptive names and readable assertions, which can improve maintainability and understandability. Despite the promises, LLM-based approaches also introduce some new challenges. Generated tests might seem reasonable yet can have incorrect or weak assertions, especially when the model “hallucinates” behavior that is not actually supported by the program (Schäfer, et al., 2023; Dakhel, et al., 2024). The output can also vary between runs, as different prompts may lead to different test cases. Sometimes the model can rely more on common patterns learned from training data than on the specific behavior of the program under test (Chen, et al., 2021; Lemieux, et al., 2023). However, research is still ongoing to improve LLM-based test generation, for example, through few-shot prompting, iterative refinement, and hybrid methods that combine LLMs with traditional testing techniques (Chen, et al., 2021; Schäfer, et al., 2023; Lemieux, et al., 2023; Dakhel, et al., 2024). Background 5 2.2 Mutation Testing Mutation testing is a fault-based testing technique that evaluates the fault-detection effectiveness of the generated test suites by measuring the suite's ability to detect artificially injected faults, called mutants (Jia & Harman, 2011). Mutation testing is based on two primary hypotheses: first the Competent Programmer Hypothesis and the Coupling Effect (DeMillo, et al., 1978; Offutt, 1989). The Competent Programmer Hypothesis, introduced by DeMillo, Lipton, and Sayward, suggests that programmers typically write programs that are close to correct. As a result, most real defects tend to be small syntactic or logical mistakes rather than major algorithmic failures (DeMillo, et al., 1978). The Coupling Effect, later introduced by Jeff Offutt (1992), states that test cases capable of detecting simple faults are also likely to detect more complex faults that are coupled with them. In other words, if a test suite can reliably detect small, artificially injected faults, it is more likely to detect subtle and real defects as well (Offutt, 1992). Under these hypotheses, a test suite that fails to detect small, artificial faults (mutants) is likely not to find real bugs. Mutation testing follows a four-stage process (Jia & Harman, 2011). First stage is the generation of the mutants, where the source code is modified by applying mutation operators. Then the existing test suite is executed against each mutant independently. Each mutant represents a separate modified version of the program. In the third step, the mutants are classified based on test results as • Killed: the test fails when run against the mutant, indicating the mutation was detected • Survived: the tests passed, indicating the mutation was not detected • Equivalent: The mutant is identical to the original program (cannot be distinguished by any test) • Problematic: The mutant causes a timeout, crash, or build failure during test execution Finally, the mutation score is calculated. The mutation score is defined as: !"#$#%&' ()&*+ = ,%--+. !"#$'#/0&#$- 12+)"#$3-+ !"#$'#/ × 100 where "Killed Mutants" shows the number of mutants detected by the test suite, and "Total Executable Mutants" refers to mutants that could be successfully generated and executed without causing framework-level failures (Jia & Harman, 2011; Ammann & Offutt, 2016). Mutation testing has been used as a quality metric for evaluating the fault detection ability of any existing test suite (DeMillo, et al., 1978). If the mutation score is low, then it indicates that the test ran without checking the code’s Background 6 behavior. The test may have high coverage, but it uses weak assertions or does not have any assertions. Mutation testing has some practical drawbacks despite being theoretically appealing. Mutation testing is widely recognized as computationally expensive, as it requires generating and executing a potentially large number of mutants against the test suite. Large codebases can produce tens of thousands of mutants, requiring hours or days of computation (Jia & Harman, 2011; Papadakis, et al., 2018). For example, equivalent mutants, which do not change observable behavior and cannot be killed by any test (Jia & Harman, 2011), and redundant mutants, which are faulty variants of a program that is functionally identical to another mutant. These are automatically detected by any test case that can detect a challenging mutant. However, as their behavior is already covered by other mutants, they do not provide new information about a test suite's quality (Mao, et al., 2019). Since the mutation test depends on test outcomes to determine whether mutants are killed, flaky tests or non-deterministic tests can compromise the validity of mutation scores and lead to unreliable conclusions (Luo, et al., 2014). Despite the challenges, research has shown that the mutation score provides a stronger indicator of fault detection effectiveness than coverage alone (Inozemtseva & Holmes, 2014). Mutation testing has become a practical method used for identifying gaps in test suites, prioritizing test improvement efforts, and comparing the effectiveness of different testing techniques. In recent research, mutation testing is being used as a guide for test generation. When surviving mutants are identified, their characteristics, like location, operator, and context, can be analyzed to find the weaknesses in the test suite. This information can then be used to generate targeted tests aimed at eliminating those gaps (Dakhel, et al., 2024). Related Work 7 3 Related Work This section covers empirical studies on automated test generation, focusing on search-based and learning-based systems. Section 3.1 explores studies analyzing evolutionary test generation methods, and Section 3.2 highlights recent research into the use of large language models for test generation. The final paragraph of Section 3.2.5 addresses shortcomings in previous comparative reviews and highlights the research areas covered by this attempt. 3.1 Evaluation of Search-Based Studies Search-based test generation has been the subject of extensive empirical research over the past decade. This section explores major research that assesses the efficacy, effectiveness, and practical use of evolutionary techniques, with a particular focus on outcomes relevant to this work. 3.1.1 The EvoSuite Benchmark: Fraser and Arcuri (2013, 2014) Fraser and Arcuri (2014) conducted one of the largest and most comprehensive empirical studies of search-based test generation to date, setting an essential precedent for future research in the field. Their work used EvoSuite, a whole-test suite evolutionary test generation tool for Java, on 110 selected open-source projects from the SF110 corpus. Their research focused on (1) the level of structural coverage achievable with evolutionary algorithms, (2) the systematic factors that limit higher coverage, (3) the generalizability of EvoSuite-based findings to other testing tools, and (4) the impact of tool selection strategy (random versus popularity-based) on empirical results (Fraser & Arcuri, 2014). The SF110 corpus consisted of 23,105 classes containing over six million lines of code, that includes a wide range of application domains, architectural patterns, and complexity levels. EvoSuite executed using a two-minute search budget with default configuration parameters. The use of a fixed budget rather than variable time limits ensured fair comparisons between subjects while reflecting genuine resource constraints in continuous integration scenarios. Coverage was calculated using branch coverage as the primary metric, which is the percentage of decision branches (including true and false outcomes) executed throughout test suite operation. Fraser and Arcuri explained their decision by noting that that branch coverage includes statement coverage and provides more detailed insight into control flow testing than method coverage. EvoSuite obtained a mean branch coverage of 71% over 23,105 classes with median 94%, standard deviation 37%. The substantial difference between the mean and median suggested a significantly skewed distribution. Most classes had very high coverage, but a fraction was found challenging to automated testing, considerably lowering the mean. This skewed distribution indicates that evolutionary algorithms succeed at code types but face systematic barriers with others. Fraser and Arcuri investigated connections between code Related Work 8 characteristics and achieved coverage to determine what makes code responsive or resistant to search-based generation. The study evaluated the correlation between coverage and the number of branches in each class and discovered a minor negative association (Pearson's r = -0.17; Fraser & Arcuri, 2014, Section V.C). While statistically significant, the small association shows that raw structural complexity alone does not fully explain coverage variability; other factors play important roles. (Fraser & Arcuri, 2014) Fraser and Arcuri's findings established several baseline expectations for search-based test generation: • High coverage: Evolutionary algorithms consistently achieve 70%+ mean coverage on typical codebases. • Bimodal Distribution: Many classes gain very high coverage (>90%), yet a subset remains challenging to test. • Environmental Sensitivity: External dependencies (files, networks, databases) can significantly limit automated generation. • Security Constraints: Code with enhanced permissions or security-sensitive actions resists automation. Fraser and Arcuri’s extensive study established a performance baseline for search-based techniques. Pynguin, as a Python adaption of EvoSuite's basic algorithms, expected to follow similar performance patterns: high coverage on independent algorithmic code and lowered coverage on code with environmental dependencies. The coverage and bidirectional distribution form estimates for Pynguin's success in this study’s evaluation. (Fraser & Arcuri, 2014) 3.1.2 Python-Specific Evaluation: Pynguin (2022) While EvoSuite established the potential of search-based generation for Java, Python's dynamic nature posed new issues that required specialized solutions. Lukasczyk and Fraser introduced Pynguin, the first advanced search-based unit test generator created specifically for Python, to address issues absent in statically typed languages. (Lukasczyk & Fraser, 2022; Lukasczyk, et al., 2023). The authors found multiple challenges related to Python's dynamic type system. • The absence of static type declarations increases the potential input area and makes it more difficult for search-based test generating methods to predict suitable input types in advance. To generate meaningful inputs, test generation requires using runtime feedback, heuristics, or type inference procedures. (Lukasczyk & Fraser, 2022) • Because of Python's dynamic and structural typing semantics, object compatibility is established at runtime using available attributes and behaviour rather than defined types. As a result, static analysis alone is unable to accurately identify valid input types. Related Work 9 • Modern Python versions provide optional type annotations, but their use varies between projects, requiring automated test generation tools which can handle both annotated and unannotated code. • Python's dynamic object construction features, such as variable-length argument lists, factory patterns, and runtime attribute manipulation, contribute to making it more challenging to automatically generate valid object instances during test generation (Lukasczyk & Fraser, 2022). In their empirical evaluation, Lukasczyk and Fraser evaluated Pynguin using a set of 118 Python modules from 17 different open-source libraries. The evaluation compared multiple search-based algorithms implemented within Pynguin, including Whole Suite, MOSA, DynaMOSA, and MIO, against a random testing baseline. The goal of this comparison was to determine whether search-based strategies provide measurable improvements in structural coverage over non-guided input generation. Search budget or timeout for test generation was set to 600 seconds per module. The findings revealed that all search-based algorithms consistently exceeded the random baseline in terms of branch coverage. DynaMOSA had the highest mean branch coverage of 68.0%, followed by MOSA (67.8%) and Whole Suite (66.9%), with the random approach coming in at 63.6%. While the improvement over random testing was small (about 4-5 percentage points), it was consistent across the modules tested and consistent with previous research in statically typed languages (Lukasczyk & Fraser, 2022). Subsequent work extended this evaluation to a larger dataset, reporting improved performance with DynaMOSA achieving a mean branch coverage of 71.6% (Lukasczyk, et al., 2023). In addition to quantitative evaluation, the authors emphasize Python-specific issues, specifically the lack of static type information. This limitation can result in the development of syntactically valid but semantically unfounded test inputs, decreasing the practical utility of created tests. The study further discovered that including type information can increase coverage results, with average improvements of 2.20% to 4.30% (Lukasczyk, et al., 2023). These findings comply with prior studies in search-based software testing, where evolutionary methods have been shown to significantly improve structural coverage over random approaches. (Fraser & Arcuri, 2014; Panichella, et al., 2015). Overall, Lukasczyk and Fraser's work supports Pynguin as an effective search-based test generation tool for Python, with coverage levels like those found for EvoSuite in Java-based systems. However, their evaluation is mostly associated with comparing search-based algorithms to random baselines. This thesis extends prior work in several directions. It explores performance on more complex modules to assess scalability in real-world situations. Furthermore, it presents a comparison with an alternative model, mutation-guided LLM-based test generation (MuTAP), which was not explored in previous Pynguin investigations. Finally, this work incorporates qualitative analysis, covering developer effort and test usability, addressing elements that were recognized but not fully studied in earlier research. Related Work 10 3.1.3 Configuration and Parameter Sensitivity Andrea Arcuri and Gordon Fraser (2013) evaluated the sensitivity of search-based test generation to configuration settings in EvoSuite, reviewing the effect of factors such as population size, crossover rate, selection technique, and search budget on test suite quality. Their findings suggest that the search budget is the most important component, and the authors believe that it may be the primary option practitioners need to actively specify. Other options can influence efficiency; however, it is generally challenging to find configurations that exceed the default settings (Arcuri & Fraser, 2013). Key Findings in the study: • Search budget dominance: The authors identify search budget as the most significant parameter, implying that it may be the only parameter practitioners should tune. • Strong default parameters : Default configurations perform exceptionally well on a wide range of subjects, but tuned configurations do not always result in major improvements. • Limited impact of other parameters: Population size, crossover rate, and selection approach have comparatively smaller and less consistent effects on coverage. • Reduced returns with increased budget: Raising the search budget usually enhances coverage, but the gains tend to fade with time, particularly under actual execution limitations. (Arcuri & Fraser, 2013) These findings imply that for fair comparison evaluations, managing the search budget is more crucial than precision parameter modification, because the budget is the "most important" element influencing performance (Arcuri & Fraser, 2013). Larger classes are significantly more challenging to cover within fixed time constraints; as shown in the prior work (Arcuri & Fraser, 2013); therefore, the research uses varying search budgets (60-900 seconds). This approach solves the primary challenge identified in the study: expanding code complexity and target numbers require proportional search effort to achieve optimal performance. 3.1.4 Usability and Maintenance of Generated Tests Shamshiri, et al. (2018) performed a controlled experiment to assess the practicality and maintainability of automatically generated tests using EvoSuite. The study featured 75 undergraduate and postgraduate students from academic institutions rather than professional programmers, which the authors acknowledge as a potential barrier to external validity. Participants were required to complete maintenance activities, such as finding and fixing defects, using either manually written or computer-generated tests. The study evaluated both effectiveness (ability to discover and fix errors) and efficiency (time essential for completing activities) (Shamshiri, et al., 2018). Related Work 11 Key findings of the study: • Comparable Effectiveness: Participants were able to find and correct errors with comparable accuracy whether they used manually written or machine-generated tests. • Reduced Efficiency: Maintenance tasks took 29% longer when applying automatically generated tests over manually written tests, showing a high usability cost. • Test Readability and Realism: While some participants scored generated tests as easy to comprehend in organized tasks, qualitative analysis revealed that developers frequently found them more difficult to follow due to excessive input values and non-intuitive execution sequences. • Assertion and Test Quality Issues : Generated tests usually depended on regression-style assertions with no evident semantic significance, leaving developers to interpret or adjust them to comprehend the intended outcome. The authors concluded that, although automated test generation might help in defect discovery, extensive manual work is still necessary during maintenance, mainly to issues with clarity and realism in generated tests. They propose that additional studies should focus on developing more meaningful and realistic scenarios for testing rather than just optimizing coverage. They also suggest that generated tests are better suited for later phases of development, when the system's behavior remains stable, or can be recreated when necessary instead of continuously maintained (Shamshiri, et al., 2018). Shamshiri et al.'s findings emphasize the relevance of developer experience and practicality while evaluating automated test generating solutions. The clear compromise between effectiveness and efficiency is especially encouraging for the incorporation of qualitative and practical metrics in this study. Building on previous research, this study systematically measures characteristics such as developer effort, required manual intervention, and test usability, in addition to common metrics such as coverage and mutation score. In addition, by comparing search-based (Pynguin) and LLM-based (MuTAP) techniques, this study evaluates whether arising models could solve the usability issues highlighted in previous studies. 3.1.5 Synthesis of Search-Based Evaluation Research Through large-scale evaluations in both Java-based and Python-based environments, clear patterns emerge regarding the performance and restrictions of search-based test generating methods (Fraser & Arcuri, 2014; Lukasczyk & Fraser, 2022; Lukasczyk, et al., 2023). Regarding established performance characteristics, evolutionary algorithms consistently deliver moderate to high structural coverage.Previous work on EvoSuite data indicates branch coverage of 70-75% (Fraser & Arcuri, 2014), Related Work 12 while Pynguin achieves 68.0% in its initial assessment and up to 71.6% in additional evaluations (Lukasczyk & Fraser, 2022; Lukasczyk, et al., 2023). Environmental dependencies have a considerable impact on coverage scales. Code that interacts with file systems, networks, or databases shows major decreases in coverage, often lower coverage in comparison to self-contained code (Fraser & Arcuri, 2014). Coverage outcomes frequently show a bimodal pattern, with many classes achieving very high coverage (>85%), with a fraction being difficult to test automatically. This is apparent in the variation between mean and median coverage values observed in empirical studies (Fraser & Arcuri, 2014; Lukasczyk & Fraser, 2022). Coverage is prone to rise notably in the early phases of the search process eventually falling as the search budget increases, which indicates decreasing returns over time. This behavior was observed during both Java and Python-based evaluations (Lukasczyk & Fraser, 2022). Turning to systematic limitations, interactions with external systems (file I/O, databases, network services) continue to be a major limitation for automated test development, often hindering the successful investigation of program behavior (Fraser & Arcuri, 2014). Search-based algorithms struggle to properly handle classes that require elaborate initialization, precise invariants, or structured inputs, particularly in dynamically typed languages like Python (Lukasczyk & Fraser, 2022; Lukasczyk, et al., 2023). Many empirical studies rely on open-source benchmarks, for example SF110 or Python project data sets, which might not accurately reflect the level of complexity of industrial systems (Fraser & Arcuri, 2014; Lukasczyk, et al., 2023). While coverage remains the primary assessment criterion, recent research has begun to incorporate mutation analysis to evaluate test effectiveness. For example, the extended Pynguin study evaluates assertion quality with mutation scores and indicates a moderate correlation between coverage and mutation efficiency (Lukasczyk, et al., 2023). 3.2 LLM-Based Test Generation Studies The development of large language models trained on extensive code libraries resulted in an innovative approach for automated test generation. This section covers recent research into the possibilities, limits, and practical uses of LLM-based test generation. Related Work 13 3.2.1 Foundational Work: Codex and Code Generation Capabilities (2021) Chen, et al. (2021) presented Codex, a GPT-based language model trained on a large corpus of publicly available source code, which includes roughly 159 GB of Python code from GitHub. The model was designed to generate executable programs from natural language descriptions, specifically function signatures and docstrings (Chen, et al., 2021). To evaluate its capacities, the authors developed the HumanEval benchmark, which includes 164 handmade programming challenges. Each task consists of a function definition and a set of unit tests used to check the functional reliability of generated answers, rather than depending on textual similarity (Chen, et al., 2021). The 12-billion-parameter Codex model achieved: • 28.8% pass@1 accuracy, indicating the probability of generating a correct solution on the first attempt. • 72.3% pass@100 accuracy, reflecting the probability of finding at least a single correct solution from 100 generated samples. A supervised fine-tuned variation, Codex-S, significantly increased performance, achieving 37.7% pass@1 and 77.5% pass@100, demonstrating the efficacy of guided instruction using high-quality code samples. Though the study's main emphasis was on code synthesis, the authors clearly indicate that Codex can be applied to associated tasks such as test generation and code completion. Being able to generate functionally accurate code from natural language requirements indicates that LLMs can capture patterns in code that enable the generation of plausible inputs and assertions from function signatures and documentation. Despite these encouraging findings, the study notes multiple limitations associated with automated test generation: • Degradation with Complexity: Performance declines when the number of operations or constraints in a problem rises, especially for tasks that need multi-step reasoning. • Specification Understanding Challenges: Codex struggles with long or high-level specifications, especially ones that require exact interpretation of numerous conditions. • Variable Binding and Logical Consistency: When several elements are present, the model struggles to precisely associate operations with variables, leading to logically incompatible results. These limitations point out challenges with applying LLMs to tasks like test oracle creation, which need exact reasoning and strict accuracy (Chen, et al., 2021). Related Work 14 3.2.2 CodaMosa: Combining LLMs with Search-Based Testing (2023) Lemieux et al. (2023) presented CodaMosa, a hybrid test generation solution for Python that enhances the Pynguin framework by incorporating large language model assistance into search-based software testing. Instead of substituting search-based testing, CodaMosa uses an LLM to assist the search process in overcoming coverage plateaus. CodaMosa begins with standard search-based test generation using MOSA and checks coverage progress throughout the search. When coverage improvement slows down, the tool queries Codex for inputs examples or test "hints" aimed at under-covered functions. These LLM-generated hints are then translated into a representation that can be included back into the Pynguin search process and then further mutated by the evolutionary algorithm. The method was evaluated on 486 Python modules from 27 projects, with subjects chosen from the Pynguin and BugsInPy datasets. Each technique was carried out many times within a 600-second search budget, and CodaMosa was evaluated against a search-based baseline (MOSA) and an LLM-only baseline (Lemieux, et al., 2023). • The findings revealed that CodaMosa obtained statistically significantly higher coverage on many more benchmarks (33.9% for improved branch coverage and 54.1% for line coverage) than it dropped coverage on, in comparison to both baselines. • Particularly, it raised coverage on 173 benchmarks compared to MOSA and 279 benchmarks compared to the LLM-only baseline, while decreasing coverage on only 10 and 4 benchmarks, correspondingly. • The study claims this improvement is due to the ability of LLM-generated suggestions to lead the search toward semantically relevant inputs that search-based testing alone cannot generate. The study's primary focus is on coverage and not mutation score or assertion quality. The authors explicitly state that they are not solving the test oracle problem, which means that the work evaluates whether created tests reach code rather than evaluating semantic correctness. The study also shows the actual impact of API latency. Waiting for Codex to respond consumed a significant part of the search budget, with typical delays equating to hundreds of seconds of lost exploration time. Furthermore, because LLM-generated code must be transformed into Pynguin's internal representation, the potential readability advantages of raw LLM output could not be directly evaluated (Lemieux, et al., 2023). 3.2.3 CoverUp: Coverage-Guided LLM Test Generation (2025) Pizzorno and Berger (2025) introduced CoverUp, a system that creates high-coverage regression tests for Python by combining coverage analysis using large language models. To focus on specific uncovered sections, the tool uses Related Work 15 an iterative feedback loop in which it runs generated tests and returns the coverage information to the LLM. CoverUp outperformed the previous level of the art such as CodaMosa, when tested on 486 Python modules from 27 projects (Pizzorno & Berger, 2025; Lemieux, et al., 2023). • Overall achieved 61.4% line coverage and 42.7% branch coverage. • The authors discovered that almost half of CoverUp's successes (49.2% of coverage ) was from the iterative refinement of prompts using coverage analysis. (Pizzorno & Berger, 2025) The study concentrated on structural efficacy of coverage rather than test oracles; therefore, mutation scores were not included. The authors noted API latency as an actual challenge and suggested future work, including mutation testing and enhanced context provided for the LLM (Pizzorno & Berger, 2025). 3.2.4 Mutation-Aware LLM Test Generation: MuTAP (2024) Moradi Dakhel et al. (2024) proposed MuTAP, a mutation-aware technique for maximizing LLM-generated unit tests via iterative promt refining. MuTAP is particularly crucial to this study since it uses mutation testing both as an evaluation tool and as a feedback mechanism for improving the results of the tests themselves. Rather than depending solely on natural language specifications, the technique is intended to work even when there is no docstring or external description of the program under test (Dakhel, et al., 2024). MuTAP operates through an iterative feedback loop. It initially creates candidate tests using an LLM, then analyses them through mutation testing, and finally refines prompts using knowledge acquired from surviving mutants. In this approach, the surviving mutants highlight flaws in existing tests, including missing edge cases, weak assertions, or unclear logic. The improved prompt is then used to create new or enhanced tests. This method is repeated periodically to improve mutation efficiency. The study evaluates MuTAP on 164 Python functions from HumanEval and conducts tests on 1,710 problematic programs from the Refactory benchmark. The HumanEval tests compare MuTAP against numerous alternatives, including Pynguin and conventional zero-shot and few-shot LLM prompting techniques (Dakhel, et al., 2024). MuTAP achieves its best recorded result on the HumanEval benchmark, with a mutation score of 93.57%, outperforming both the Pynguin and conventional prompting baselines. The study discovered that MuTAP can identify up to 28% more problematic human-written code snippets, while Pynguin and conventional prompting techniques missed 17% of these problems. MuTAP's main contribution is that it uses mutation feedback as a focused signal for refining. Earlier LLM-based techniques were typically based on one- Related Work 16 or few-shot prompting or on coverage feedback. Alternatively, MuTAP uses surviving mutants to identify weak points in the created tests and guides the model toward more fault-finding test cases. This makes the approach particularly relevant to the Oracle problem, because even syntactically perfect tests may fail to uncover complex flaws. The authors note that the current solution is exclusive to Python, and more research on larger real-world software platforms needs to be done. Furthermore, while MuTAP demonstrates execution time, its consistency is limited because its original implementation relied on proprietary LLMs. The study also discusses benchmarks such as HumanEval and Refactory, which do not entirely represent the complexity of industrial systems with many dependencies or persistent states. Finally, although MuTAP enhances mutation efficiency, it still needs post-processing, as LLM-generated tests may have syntactic or semantic defects that often needs correction before evaluation (Dakhel, et al., 2024). 3.2.5 Synthesis of LLM-Based Test Generation Research Across fundamental work on code synthesis, comparative assessments of LLM-generated tests, hybrid search-LLM approaches, and mutation-aware refining techniques, some recurrent patterns emerged in the literature. Chen, et al. (2021) demonstrated that large language models trained on code can produce functionally accurate programs using natural-language descriptions, displaying strong code comprehension abilities on HumanEval (Chen, et al., 2021). Later studies elaborated on this approach by demonstrating that LLMs can build tests directly from source code, signatures, and usage samples, usually without task-specific fine-tuning (Schäfer, et al., 2023; Dakhel, et al., 2024). On established capabilities, the first consistent observation is that LLM-based techniques appear to capture semantic patterns in code. They frequently create natural-looking tests and non-trivial assertions by inferring the expected behavior from function signatures, implementations, and documentation. Schäfer, et al. observe that LLM-generated JavaScript tests tend to incorporate meaningful assertions that exercise meaningful aspects of program behavior rather than just repeating observed results. Similarly, MuTAP suggests that iterative refinement led by mutation feedback can improve mutation efficiency compared to one-shot generation (Schäfer, et al., 2023; Dakhel, et al., 2024). A second recurring pattern is that feedback increases quality. In hybrid systems like CodaMosa, LLM guiding helps search-based testing escape coverage plateaus by injecting semantically helpful hints when standard search misses. In MuTAP, surviving mutants use themselves as a targeted feedback signal to modify prompts and increase fault detecting ability. These studies indicate that LLMs tend to perform better when paired with structured feedback rather than used alone in a single zero-shot pass (Lemieux, et al., 2023; Dakhel, et al., 2024). Related Work 17 A third observation is readability and naturalness. The research frequently describes LLM-produced tests as more natural-looking than many standard generated tests, but this advantage is frequently mentioned qualitatively rather than through a single shared quantitative metric. Concurrently, claims on readability should be kept moderate because research like Schäfer et al. focused more on coverage and efficacy than on systematic human-subject evaluation of maintainability (Schäfer, et al., 2023). Despite these advantages, a few limitations are still evident in many studies. Variable structural efficiency is one. While LLM-based techniques can outperform conventional feedback-directed or random baselines in certain contexts and do well on benchmarks, they do not always outperform search-based methods in every task. The reason hybrid approaches like CodaMosa were developed is that pure LLM generation might not be able to meet difficult coverage requirements without further search-based refinement (Schäfer, et al., 2023; Lemieux, et al., 2023) Another recurring challenge is correctness and executability. Syntax mistakes, incorrect assumptions, invalid API usage, and assertions that fail to run correctly without repair can all be found in LLM-generated tests. Schäfer et al. observe non-trivial proportions of failed generated tests that need correction or recurrence and Moradi Dakhel, et al. specifically note the fact that generated tests frequently need post-processing since they may contain syntactic or functional errors (Schäfer, et al., 2023; Dakhel, et al., 2024). The simplicity and scope of benchmarks is a further limitation. Many significant assessments rely on benchmarks including package-level API tasks or HumanEval, which are valuable but do not accurately reflect vast, stateful, dependency-heavy industrial systems. While CodaMosa assesses on Python modules from Pynguin and BugsInPy datasets, MuTAP evaluates on HumanEval and Refactory. These are more comprehensive, but they still differ significantly from enterprise production code. Concerns about cost and reproducibility are also raised by the studies. Several techniques rely on proprietary models or commercial APIs, which add latency, token expenses, and limited long-term reproducibility. CodaMosa explicitly discusses API delay as a practical bottleneck, and MuTAP’s original implementation also depends on external LLM infrastructure (Lemieux, et al., 2023; Dakhel, et al., 2024). Taken together, the literature reveals a broad trade-off between technical effectiveness and practical usability, though the boundary is not fixed. Although search-based techniques can achieve large coverage with adequate search budgets and are effective at systematic structural exploration, the resulting tests may be more challenging to understand and maintain. In comparison, LLM-based tools often generate tests that appear more natural and are semantically richer, but they may need to be corrected, may be less stable between runs, and may not reliably reach challenging execution paths without additional input or search. CodaMosa and MuTAP are examples of hybrid and mutation-aware techniques that are promising since they integrate Related Work 18 structured guiding with semantic development (Lemieux, et al., 2023; Dakhel, et al., 2024). Several gaps remain despite this progress. First, there are a few studies that compare search-based and LLM-based techniques in a controlled paired design with identical realistic Python subjects. Second, industrial and dependency-heavy code is not sufficiently investigated as most evaluations continue to be benchmark-centered. Third, compared to coverage or mutation score, practical issues like manual intervention, setup difficulty, execution overhead, and deployment effort are still not as thoroughly assessed. Finally, even though Python is now more widely covered due to tools like CodaMosa and MuTAP, there is still limited information on how these methods perform on larger real-world Python codebases outside of carefully selected research benchmarks (Lemieux, et al., 2023; Dakhel, et al., 2024). This study addresses these gaps by evaluating a mutation-aware LLM-based method (MuTAP) alongside a search-based tool (Pynguin) on real Python code under controlled conditions, while also considering important factors like developer effort, user intervention, and constraints related to local model deployment. Methodology 19 4 Methodology 4.1 Overview and Research Design This study uses a comparative evaluation structure to thoroughly assess two different automated unit test generation approaches - Pynguin, a search-based testing tool, and MuTAP, a mutation-aware large language model-based test generator. The research design connects theoretical concepts in automated test generation with practical experimentation, enabling systematic comparison of the two approaches across multiple dimensions, including test quality, computational efficiency, performance across different code domains, and developer experience. The experimental design has been structured to ensure reproducibility through consistent execution environments, defined tool setups, and specified assessment procedures. This controlled environment offers a fair comparison of fundamentally different methods for automated test generation. Both tools are assessed on the same subject codebases using the same mutation testing framework, along with thorough documentation of configuration choices, necessary adjustments, and any manual interventions required during execution. By standardizing evaluation conditions, the research ensures that the findings reflect tool behavior rather than environmental variation while acknowledging the distinctive characteristics of search-based and LLM-based approaches. 4.2 Research Questions and Objectives The study is designed around four key research questions aimed at complementary areas of automated test-generating tool performance and effectiveness. RQ1. How does test quality, measured through mutation testing, compare between search-based and LLM-based generation approaches? Evaluates whether one tool consistently discovers more mutations than the other, and whether this remains constant across different code structures and complexity levels. Addresses the fundamental effectiveness of every approach to generate tests capable of finding defects represented by mutants. RQ2. What are the computational efficiency trade-offs in terms of time and resource consumption? Assesses that test generation effectiveness must be balanced against practical constraints in software development environments. The analysis considers both automated execution costs and human effort required for tool configuration and troubleshooting. RQ3. How do these tools perform across different code contexts (open source vs. corporate)? Evaluates results by separately analysing open-source and industrial modules, examining mutation score, coverage metrics, and execution characteristics. Methodology 20 Understanding domain-specific performance enables elaborate tool choices for professionals working in different contexts. RQ4. What is the practical usability experience, including setup complexity and required manual intervention? Measures through documented manual interventions, troubleshooting, configuration complexity, and failure rates. Developer experience factors are essential to decide whether tools can be used in real development workflows beyond controlled experimental environments. Beyond these primary research questions, the study examines additional dimensions to better understand the behavior and limitations of each tool. These include identifying common failure modes, analysing operator-level surviving mutant patterns, measuring execution time at the test generation level, and evaluating test code structural quality. These additional perspectives contextualise the main findings and clarify practical trade-offs between the two approaches. The primary objective of this research is to conduct a systematic comparison of the test generation capabilities of Pynguin and MuTAP. This study evaluates the quality of generated tests using mutation testing, examines efficiency in terms of both computational cost and developer effort, and analyzes how tool performance varies across different code contexts, including open-source and industrial codebases. These goals are addressed through controlled experimentation designed to ensure fair comparison while acknowledging the fundamental architectural differences between search-based and LLM-based approaches. In addition to these primary objectives, the study aims to identify the strengths and limitations of each tool. It also evaluates the practical challenges associated with installation, configuration, and execution in realistic development environments. By combining technical evaluation with usability considerations, the research aims to give meaningful, evidence-based insights for professionals considering the implementation of automated test-generating tools. 4.3 Methodological Design Choices We used a paired comparison method for this research, in which both tools are run on the same set of subject modules under carefully controlled environment (Arcuri & Briand, 2014; Wohlin, et al., 2012). Running the tools on identical codebases reduces confounding factors and allows identified performance differences to be traced more directly to the characteristics of each tool than to differences in the environment or subject complexity (Kitchenham, et al., 2002). The design supports better causal inference on the relative performance of search-based as opposed to LLM-based test generating techniques by ensuring consistent evaluation conditions across tools. Choosing a paired comparison design is consistent with established empirical software engineering practices. This approach is particularly relevant considering the limited number of suitable subject modules available for this study, as paired designs enhance comparability and reduce the influence of confounding variables when sample numbers are limited, making observed Methodology 21 variations between tools more attributable to tool characteristics than to subject variation (Wohlin, et al., 2012; Kitchenham, et al., 2002; Arcuri & Briand, 2014). All experiments were conducted locally in the same environment, with both tools running under identical hardware and software conditions. Using a single, consistent execution environment decreases the uncertainty caused by differences in system load, hardware setup, and network conditions. This design prioritizes internal validity, allowing for a more accurate attribution of performance differences to the tools themselves rather than external factors. While this approach restricts claims about performance across different deployment environments, it improves the reliability of direct comparisons in the context of this study. For a fair evaluation, all generated test suites were run through two standardized mutation testing frameworks, mutmut and MutPy. The use of multiple mutation engines reduces dependency on a single mutation implementation and allows cross-validation of mutation-based findings. Mutmut was selected as the primary mutation analysis engine due to its stable execution across subjects and its support for larger, systematically generated mutant sets. MutPy was additionally used as a supplementary mutation framework to test the reliability of results under an alternative mutation implementation. As mutation frameworks differ in terms of operator selection, mutant generation method, and execution outcome classification, outcomes are listed with detailed mutant data to ensure transparency and comparability. 4.4 Subject Selection The study's experimental dataset consists of two categories: an open-source benchmark using modules from popular Python libraries and an industrial benchmark with anonymized modules from a real-world software system. These two routes provide complementing coverage, with the first giving external reliability through publicly verifiable code and the second providing environmental credibility through code that is reflective of production software. text: Beyond Coverage: Automatic Test Suite Augmentation for Enhanced Effectiveness using Large Language Models ZEYU LU, Nanjing University, China PENG ZHANG∗, Nanjing University, China YUGE NIE, Nanjing University, China YIBIAO YANG∗, Nanjing University, China YUTIAN TANG, University of Glasgow, United Kingdom CHUN YONG CHONG, Monash University Malaysia, Malaysia YUMING ZHOU∗, Nanjing University, China Large Language Models (LLMs) have gained significant traction in software engineering for automating tasks such as unit test generation. Most existing studies prioritize code coverage as the primary metric for enhancing test suite effectiveness. However, prior research has shown that although code coverage can reach approximately 80%, the mutation score, which generally exhibits a stronger correlation with defect detection effectiveness, attains only about 35%. This gap highlights the need to enhance test suite effectiveness guided by mutation score rather than code coverage. Recent studies, including MuTAP and MutGen, explored the use of survived mutants to enhance test suite effectiveness. However, their evaluations were limited to simple standalone methods that rely on built-in functions and standard libraries. Non-standalone methods, which depend on other classes and involve complex user-defined types, are more intricate and commonly found in real-world projects. The limited contextual information and basic repair mechanisms in their prompt designs make it unclear whether their performance can generalize to non-standalone methods. Moreover, the two studies rely on existing language-specific, rule-based mutation techniques, which require specific configurations and incur additional costs when adapting to other programming languages. To bridge this gap, we propose a novel, fully automatic LLM-based approach to enhance test suite effec- tiveness, guided by survived mutants. The approach augments initial test suites by integrating mutation testing with test case generation. It takes focal method information as input and generates test cases targeting survived mutants identified from applying the initial test suites. Our approach incorporates multiple prompt techniques, rich contextual information, and an advanced repair mechanism to effectively generate test cases for non-standalone methods. The evaluation covers 1,035 focal methods, categorized as standalone or non-standalone. On average, the mutation score increases by 16.04% for standalone methods and 8.11% for non-standalone methods. We validate the practical impact of augmented test suites in LLM-based code generation. After test suite augmentation, pass@1 decreased by 0.3152 and 0.1772 on average for standalone and non-standalone methods, respectively, indicating the effectiveness of our approach in reducing false positives caused by insufficient test cases in code generation evaluation. Lang. 10, OOPSLA1, Article 143 (April 2026), 29 pages. https://doi.org/10.1145/3798251 1 Introduction Unit testing plays a fundamental and crucial role in ensuring software quality. While unit tests can be generated manually, this process requires significantly more human effort. Over the years, numerous techniques for automatically generating test cases have been proposed. These techniques can be categorized into random testing (e.g., Randoop [59]), constraint-based testing (e.g., KLEE [16]), and search-based testing (e.g., EvoSuite [27]). Additionally, some studies generate test cases using model checkers [64] or learning-based approaches [73]. Recently, large language models (LLMs) [5, 14, 91] have gained popularity and brought transfor- mative changes to the software engineering community. LLMs for generating unit test cases have the advantage of statically generating test cases based on given focal methods and being easily adaptable to multiple programming languages. Several studies [82, 85] have explored the use of LLMs for test case generation, revealing that directly generating test cases with LLMs often results in low code coverage. To overcome these limitations, various approaches have been proposed, including chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting [85] and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) [90], to enhance the code coverage of LLM-generated test cases. Other approaches [7, 33, 47, 51, 61, 86] focus on generating test cases using feedback from code coverage information, targeting uncovered branches or paths in the focal methods to improve code coverage. With these enhancement tech- niques, previous studies [18, 33, 69, 78, 85, 90] have shown significantly improved code coverage of LLM-generated test cases. However, most research on LLM-based test case generation focuses primarily on enhancing code coverage. Two commonly used metrics for assessing the defect detection effectiveness of a test suite are code coverage and mutation score. Code coverage measures the proportion of code elements, such as statements and branches, executed by a test suite relative to the total number of code elements. Mutation score, on the other hand, evaluates the proportion of mutants (artificially introduced variations of the program under test) that are killed by a test suite relative to the total number of generated mutants. Pan et al. [61] measured the mutation score achieved by LLM-generated test cases for Java projects and found that the mutation score ranged from 2% to 35%, even though the achieved statement coverage and branch coverage could reach nearly 80%. Compared to code coverage, most studies [12, 43] show that mutation score correlates more strongly with the defect detection effectiveness of test suites. Consequently, the mutation score, computed from the generated mutants, is a more effective metric for enhancing the effectiveness of test suites [63, 65, 67]. The need to enhance test suite effectiveness is recognized in datasets proposed for evaluating code understanding [34, 44, 54, 80] and code generation [24, 36, 44, 80, 87] tasks, where LLMs help reduce extensive human effort. Datasets in which focal methods are categorized as standalone (self-contained, invoking or accessing built-in functions or standard libraries) or non-standalone (with project-level or external API dependencies). In code generation tasks, test cases play a crucial role in ensuring the correctness of the generated code. However, many datasets [49, 50] highlight the ineffectiveness of test suites in evaluating code generation by LLMs. The evaluation of generated code may yield false positives, in which incorrect implementations are deemed correct due to Proc. ACM Program. Lang., Vol. 10, No. OOPSLA1, Article 143. Publication date: April 2026. Beyond Coverage: Automatic Test Suite Augmentation for Enhanced Effectiveness using Large Language Models 143:3 insufficient test cases. A previous study [50] reported that the estimated false positive rate of the HumanEval dataset [17] is 30%, while that of the APPS dataset [37] is considerably higher at 60%. Efforts have been made to augment existing test suites in datasets used to evaluate code gen- eration capabilities. In previous studies, initial test suites were typically constructed from sim- ple human-written or programming competition problems, and additional tests were generated to reduce false positives. These studies commonly generate new test cases by executing newly created inputs and deriving valid outputs through consistency checks across multiple code sam- ples. For example, AlphaCode [ 50] and EvalPlus [ 52] rely on mutating test inputs to generate additional test cases. Similarly, TACO [ 49] uses LLMs to supplement test cases by generating additional inputs for correct code samples and capturing their corresponding outputs. This ap- proach works well for standalone methods with simple inputs and outputs, such as primitive types, strings, or collections. However, it is hardly applicable to datasets like CoderEval [84] and ComplexCodeEval [25], which contain non-standalone methods from real projects. Such methods often involve complex types (e.g., user-defined classes or interfaces within a project), making it difficult to generate new inputs and corresponding outputs in the same way. For example, a non-standalone method may have a test case with an assertion such as: assertThatThrownBy(() -> ServiceParser.getServiceInstanceName(null)).isInstanceOf(NullPointerException.class); Moreover, these studies lack general guidance for enhancing the sufficiency of test cases. For example, the TACO augmentation approach produced an average of over 200 tests, but this number is not universally applicable as guidance across all code generation tasks. Test suite size is an unrealistic objective for constructing test suites [19]. On the contrary, test adequacy criteria are considered a stopping rule that determines whether sufficient testing has been conducted and measures testing adequacy with respect to software testing requirements [92]. Code coverage or mutation score, measured based on test adequacy criteria, are widely deemed as proxies for test suite effectiveness [8, 12, 29–31, 43]. Enhancing test suite effectiveness guided by mutation score is more advantageous, as mutation score is generally a more reliable indicator of defect detection effectiveness than code coverage, and test suite size is an unrealistic objective for test suite construction. Recent studies, such as MuTAP [21] and MutGen [77], generate test cases targeting survived mutants to improve the mutation score. However, the two studies suffer from three limitations: (L1) Insufficient evaluation. The focal methods used in MuTAP and MutGen are standalone and relatively simple, whereas real-world projects commonly involve non-standalone methods. Yu et al. [84] report that non-standalone methods account for more than 70% of methods in 100 popular Java and Python GitHub projects. Since focal methods in practical projects are typically non-standalone and more complex, the performance ofMuTAP and MutGen on real-world projects remains unclear. (L2) Simplistic prompt design. Compared with standalone methods, testing non-standalone methods may require mocks or stubs and contextual information from the entire project. The simplistic prompt design of MuTAP and MutGen, characterized by limited contextual information and a basic repair mechanism, could constrain their applicability to non-standalone methods. (L3) Constrained adaptability. The mutation testing in MuTAP and MutGen is conducted as a separate process that relies on existing rule-based mutation tools, which are highly syntax- dependent and demand specific configuration. This reliance incurs significant costs when adapting to other programming languages. In this study, we propose a fully automatic LLM-based approach guided by survived mutants that enhances the effectiveness of test suites. Our evaluation covers both standalone and non-standalone methods, filling the gap of prior studies that lack real-world project evaluation(addressing L1). The approach combines mutation testing with test suite augmentation. It operates by taking information Proc. ACM Program. Lang., Vol. 10, No. OOPSLA1, Article 143. First, we use LLMs to generate mutants for focal methods. The code understanding capabilities of LLMs enable mutations to be conducted at the semantic level rather than the syntactic level. The mutant generation approach is designed to cover various behaviors of a focal method and to produce survived mutants. The approach requires neither training nor fine-tuning, is language-independent, and is readily adaptable for multi-language mutant generation (addressing L3). Next, the survived mutants are used to guide the test case generation. To maximize the number of test cases that kill survived mutants, we employ multiple techniques, including CoT and RAG, during the test suite augmentation process. Class-level and project-level contextual information is incorporated into the prompts to further support effective test suite augmentation. Static analysis guides LLMs in repairing test cases through error message parsing and annotations (addressing L2). Existing studies [18, 78, 85] that utilize LLMs for test case generation typically generate test cases from scratch, regardless of whether an initial test suite exists. In contrast, our approach augments the initial test suite of a focal method, thereby enhancing its initial mutation score, which refers to the mutation score achieved by the initial test suite prior to augmentation, and could complement these studies. If no test cases are available for a focal method, existing LLM-based test case generation techniques can be employed to construct an initial test suite. Our contributions can be summarized as follows: • We propose a novel approach for generating mutants using LLMs tailored to test suite augmentation. The approach focuses on semantic-level mutation and is language-independent, requiring no training or fine-tuning. • We introduce a fully automatic LLM-based approach to enhance the effectiveness of initial test suites guided by survived mutants. The average mutation score increases by 16.04% for standalone methods and by 8.11% for non-standalone methods. The results on GitHub projects (i.e., non-standalone methods) indicate the practical applicability of the proposed approach. • The augmentation approach offers a way to alleviate the false positive problem in existing datasets for code generation tasks. After augmentation, the pass@1 decreased by 0.3152 and 0.1772 on average for standalone and non-standalone focal methods, respectively, indicating reduced false positives in code generation evaluation. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 offers a review of the background and prior work. Section 3 describes the proposed approach for mutation testing and test suite augmentation. Section 4 details the experimental setup and presents the results for both the proposed approach and the baselines. Section 5 reports additional experimental results and discusses threats to validity. Section 6 offers concluding remarks. 2 Background and Related Work 2.1 Mutant Generation Rule-based approaches, such as PIT [20], are widely used and rely on predefined mutation operators that are applied to specific program elements. Rule-based mutant generation approaches rely on predefined transformation rules, which inherently limit mutation diversity. Although such approaches are effective at producing structurally valid mutants, they may fail to generate semantic- level mutants and struggle to approximate realistic developer errors. Learning-based approaches generate mutants by leveraging knowledge learned from large corpora of real-world bugs during training [70, 74, 75]. Proc. ACM Program. Lang., Vol. 10, No. OOPSLA1, Article 143. Publication date: April 2026. Beyond Coverage: Automatic Test Suite Augmentation for Enhanced Effectiveness using Large Language Models 143:5 Recently, pre-trained LLMs have gained significant popularity, and several studies have explored their use for mutant generation. The code understanding capabilities of LLMs enable the genera- tion of semantic-level mutants that better reflect natural human error patterns. 𝜇BERT [22] uses CodeBERT [26] to generate mutants by performing code completion for masked tokens. Similarly, LLMorpheus [71] generates mutants by prompting LLMs to perform code completion for JavaScript code. Beyond using code completion to generate mutants, MetaMut [57] leverages LLMs to generate mutation operators, which are then used to mutate C programs, and LLMut [ 76] uses LLMs to generate mutants for a single line of code. These studies [22, 57, 71, 76] focus on generating mutants without considering the killability of the generated mutants. In contrast, Ibrahimzada et al. [39] proposed BugFarm, which focuses on generating hard-to-kill mutants. They utilize the attention mechanism of pre-trained transformer models to identify the least attended program locations, then prompt LLMs to generate mutants. However, BugFarm requires fine-tuning to determine the least attended locations, which incurs additional time and resource costs. 2.2 Effectiveness of LLM-Based Test Case Generation Among traditional approaches, symbolic execution [13, 41] enables systematic path exploration for test case generation and offers theoretical formal guarantees: a satisfying assignment produced by an SMT (Satisfiability Modulo Theories) solver ensures that the corresponding input executes the target path in the program. However, symbolic execution faces significant challenges. Even with environment modeling, SMT solvers often struggle with path constraints involving non-primitive types or external interactions, such as file systems or networking. In addition, symbolic execution typically generates only test inputs and does not provide expected outputs or behavioral oracles. Although LLM-based test case generation may suffer from hallucinations and lacks such formal guarantees, LLMs’ code understanding capabilities enable them to handle complex dependencies and infer plausible expected behaviors to form assertions. Numerous studies [7, 18, 21, 33, 47, 51, 61, 66, 68, 69, 78, 81–83, 85, 86, 90] have explored the use of LLMs for test case generation. We categorize these studies from the following perspectives: Enhancing Pass Rate: The test cases generated by LLMs suffer from a low pass rate, primarily due to compilation and execution errors [85]. To improve pass rates, most studies [7, 18, 21, 33, 47, 61, 68, 69, 78, 85, 90] adopt various approaches to repair the generated test cases. The effectiveness of test suites is then measured based on the passed test cases. Achieved Test Suite Effectiveness: Several studies, such as ChatUniTest [18], measure code coverage achieved after test case generation. Pan et al. [61] proposed aster and evaluated the code coverage and mutation score of test cases generated by LLMs for Java and Python classes or modules. For their results on Java projects, the statement and branch coverage of the generated test suites could reach nearly 80%, while the mutation score reached a maximum of 35%. The significantly lower mutation score of the generated test suites highlights the need for further enhancement to improve their effectiveness. Enhancing Test Suite Effectiveness: Existing studies employ various methods to improve test suite effectiveness. (1) Code Coverage. To enhance code coverage, different approaches have been proposed, including method-invocation analysis [81], CoT prompting [85], the combination of LLMs and symbolic execution [66], focal method slicing [78], RAG [90], and reinforcement learning [86]. Additionally, aster [61], TestART [33], TestCTRL [86], CoverUp [7], STRUT [51], and YATE [47] improve test suite effectiveness by relying on feedback from code coverage. (2) Mutation Score. When evaluating test suite effectiveness, the mutation score has been shown to be a more reliable predictor of the defect detection effectiveness of test suites than code coverage [43]. To generate more effective test suites, it is preferable to adopt mutation score-guided test Proc. ACM Program. Lang., Vol. 10, No. OOPSLA1, Article 143. MuTAP [21] and MutGen [77] utilize survived mutants to generate test cases. However, their effectiveness on complex, practical code remains unclear. 3 Approach 3.1 Overview Fig. 1. Approach overview. The approach integrates mutation testing and test suite augmentation, where survived mutants from SUNG guide test case generation via RAGTIME. Figure 1 presents an overview of our approach, which includes SUNG (LLMs for Semantic-level mUtaNt Generation) and RAGTIME (LLMs for suRvived mutAnts Guided Test suIte augMEntation). Given a focal method and the test cases that test it, we use SUNG to perform mutation testing. If any mutants survive, we use RAGTIME to generate new test cases to kill these survived mutants. The newly generated test cases are then merged with the initial test cases to form the augmented test suite. The entire process of our approach, including mutation testing and test suite augmentation, relies solely on in-context learning of LLMs and is fully automatic. Since LLMs are trained on multiple programming languages, our approach can be easily adapted to different programming languages. 3.2 SUNG We propose SUNG, which uses LLMs to generate mutants based on program semantics and then conducts mutation testing. Algorithm 1 illustrates the procedure of SUNG. 3.2.1 Mutant Generation. We generate mutants tailored to the scenario to enhance the effectiveness of test suites based on survived mutants. First, we aim to generate mutants to enable the generation of test cases that exercise all possible behaviors of a focal method. Second, we aim to generate as many survived mutants as possible to guide the generation of additional test cases. Approach. Mutant generation is conducted using six distinct sub-approaches (line 1 in Algorithm 1). While each sub-approach in SUNG operates largely independently, the six sub-approaches collectively function as an integrated whole. Sub-Approach 1: Behavior Model.Mutant generation in this sub-approach is designed to encompass various program behaviors. Since this issue cannot be fully resolved at present [58], we follow a previous study [68] to address the problem through repetitive runs. Specifically, the process of mutant generation is repeated three times (line 1 in Algorithm 1), and the mapping of mutations back to the complete focal method is also repeated (line 7 in Algorithm 1). All mutants generated across these three iterations are combined to form the final set of mutants. We avoid excessive repetitions (e.g., 10) to mitigate the high cost associated with invoking the LLM API. For test suite augmentation, we prompt LLMs to generate three distinct test cases each time during both the generation and repair phases. The augmentation process is not repeated, as the three augmentation steps for each classified group of survived mutants, combined with iterating over all groups, help ensure comprehensive test case generation. Another reason is the significant token consumption and time required to generate and execute test cases against survived mutants. 4 Evaluation 4.1 Experimental Setup 4.1.1 Research Questions.
